Trunk Railway system. speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Montreal Star, on the 23rd instant, published an appeal to the Senate as to what it should do with this Bill, and it declared that this House and the majority supporting the Government are " jamming through, during the dying days of a special session called for another purpose, a measure which many Canadians believe spells ruin for their land. The Government of the day has no mandate for the Grand Trunk purchase. It has been able to give no adequate reason for the questionable urgency of its ' haste to force the deal
through."	.	.
So my hon. friends opposite who ]eer at the word "jam" may possibly now see that they are not in the company of their own friends. I do not usually attach vast importance to what the Montreal Star says, but I am bound to say that my hon. friends opposite should pay more respect to its opinion than they are disposed to do today.	,
This Bill passed through committee last evening. It is not usual in a matter of so much importance to proceed immediately with the third reading of the Bill. I think there will be no case found where, against the protests of the Opposition, a Bill of this character has been proceeded with so quickly. However, the Government are responsible for that and they must take the responsibility. Another reason is this: I think it will seldom be found that a measure of this importance, a measure of a controversial character, has been brought

to a division on a Friday, when it is well known that many members on both sides find it convenient to go home, and therefore are not able to participate in the proceedings. True they may be playing truant, but still the fact remains that the truancy is not confined to one side or the other. Members who live within easy distance of Ottawa may be excused if, at the week-end, they should go home to visit their families. I can understand that those at a distance, like my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) have a different view. On this .question of going home we have had a change of front. We have had a pathetic statement by the Minister of Railways attributing to us on this side a desire "to go home." Norw the cry is heard on the other side; it is hon. gentlemen opposite who say, "let us get through and go home." Hon. gentlemen opposite have suddenly become anxious to go home. They have suddenly joined in this desire of the Government to jam this Bill through in the manner described by the Conservative Montreal Star. What reason has been given for this extraordinary proceeding with respect to a measure brought down in the last days of a session, a session called for a special purpose and not for this purpose at all? My hon. friends opposite are blowing hot and cold on this question of this special session. When we bring forward any new business, when we suggest that there may be some other questions to discuss, they say. "Oh this is a special session, we have nothing to do but the work of the special session." And yet when the work of the special session was completed, and when the members were about ready to go home, when, in fact, the leader of the Government told the members to pack their trunks and get out,-

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I said the hope was entertained.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that was the "hope" with regard to prorogation, so far as the Government were concerned- at all events the expectation was that prorogation would be reached within a couple of days. Is there any reason for this extraordinary proceeding? It would be incorrect to say there is no reason and I always like to be accurate in my statements in the House. It would be incorrect to say the Government have given no reason; they did give a reason. The President of the Privy Council-I am sorry he is not here to-day but he is absent on public business -gave us a reason and a reason apparently very convincing to himself and to his friends around him. The President of the Privy Council said that if this business was not rushed through now there would be opposition developed in the country-if this business is not pushed through now opposition will be organized. That is to say, if the people of this country had an opportunity of understanding this measure, then surely there would be a manifestation of public opinion against it, and therefore he said: Let us stifle public opinion; let us rush the thing through while we can and before the public can understand the true nature of the measure. Now, in so far as this is a question of public ownership I think the men-the thousands of men- who honestly believe in public ownership- and I know there are such, including a great many men in this House, although not all who are going to vote for this Bill-the thousands of men all over this country who believe in public ownership might well hesitate before asking the Government to carry this measure at the present time. I do not want to argue against public ownership. I only ask the House to admit that this matter of public ownership, as applied to the great railways of the country, is a large and important question upon which a great many of the wisest men in this country entertain a serious difference of opinion. Is it too much to say that? It is a well-known fact that while public ownership may be admitted in some cases, as applied to the great railways of the country, there is a strong feeling among those whom I have described as among the gravest and best of our people in this country who sincerely feel that this is a dangerous measure. All I ask the House to admit is this: That in view of that serious division of opinion which exists, in view of the gravity of the question, we might well hesitate to take the tremendous plunge proposed in this Bill. We now have 14,000



miles of railway under the control and
operation of the Canadian Government. That is a pretty big order; that is a pretty big opportunity for testing the merits of public ownership. I believe that when I say we should for the present rest content with that, that we should operate that 14,000 miles of railway for a little while, that we should prove if we can by experience that public ownership is able to justify itself-1 believe when I say that that would be a wise policy, I am saying a thing with which the sober-minded people of this country will agree. Fourteen thousand miles to-day under government ownership; yet we are asked to plunge into this large Grand Trunk enterprise.
I feel, Sir, that the information which has been given to the House on this subject is entirely inadequate. Members of the Government have shown plainly that they have not that knowledge of the question which they ought to have in dealing with so vast a measure. The discussion that has taken place, the answers that have been given to questions, all go to show that there has been a regrettable lack of information. I do not blame the Government much on that account; they could not, in such a short time, acquire the information. This Grand Trunk Railway system is a vast railway system, including railways, steamships, hotels'. There are many subsidiary companies, interwoven one with the other; there are financial communications between them; the whole system is one that no ordinary man could understand except after long study.
Now, there has been no adequate investigation into the condition of this Grand Trunk system. The only pretense at investigation-I will not call it a pretense at investigation, because for its own purposes it was a good investigation-the only investigation we have had in the matter is that of what is commonly called the Dray-ton-Acworth Commission. That commission investigated railway matters about three years ago. I think the inquiry took place towards the end of 1916, and in the spring of 1917 they made their report. That was a report on the railway conditions of the country generally, and, of course, it included a reference to the Grand Trunk.
Now, what information do we get from that report? In the Bill before the House we are dealing largely with the value of the stocks of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and its subsidiaries. The only report to which we can look with any degree of intelligence in this matter is the Drayton-Acworth re-
port, brought in under the circumstances that I have described. And what do they say? As respects the value of these stocks -and that is the main question in this Bill, after all-the Drayton-Acworth report says:
Even if the Government were to relieve them entirely, as suggested by their President, of their unfortunate Grand Trunk Pacific venture -and, as we have already said, we cannot think that the request can be reasonably Justified-it is evident that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not and will not be for some time to come in a position enabling it to pay out any money at all in dividends. We regard the entire share capital as being intrinsically qf but small value at the (present time. On the basis of present value of maintainable lffSome the fair compensation would be very small.
That is the report of the Drayton-Acworth Commission:	That all this share capital
of the Grand Trunk is worth very little; to use their own words, it is of " but small value." These stocks, which the only valuable report available describes as of small value, we, by the action we are asked to take to-day, are converting into a large and extravagant value. We are taking no less than $60,000,000 of these stocks and giving them what is practically a par value by undertaking to guarantee four per cent on them forever. As respects the vast sum of upwards of $180,000,000 of these stocks which the Drayton-Acworth report states are of small value, we are going to submit that to all the doubts and uncertainties of arbitration.
All the information, then, that we have as to the value of these stocks and which is entitled to respect on this question comes from the Drayton-Acworth report; and that report, submitted by a commission of which the present Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) was a member, tells us that these stocks are of very little value. We are asked to convert them into a value of at least $60,000,000 as respects one stock, and heaven only knows what value may be assigned by the arbitrators to the others. It is on information of that character, on a situation like that, that we are asked today to adopt this Bill. I believe, that the sober sense of the country will say that we have not the knowledge, we have not the information, which would enable the House or the country to understand this matter.
The matter, Sir, is not being well understood in the country. I do not wonder that the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) says that if there be delay there will be opportunity for opposition. Take what has occurred in the city of Montreal. A Board of Trade is not always the highest exponent of public opinion; its members are only human and they make mistakes. But when

you get a body of men who are exceptionally well qualified to deal with business propositions, a body of men who are usually divided, as all men are, on questions of trade and politics; when you get a body of men of that kind absolutely unanimous in condemning a measure of this character, I say that you have a conclusion to which you are bound to attach respect. The Board of Trade of Montreal did not act in a hurry. They passed their resolution, and they sent a delegation to Ottawa who interviewed the ministers and received the benefit of such information and such assurances as the ministers could give them. The delegation went back to Montreal and made a report to the Board. The Board again assembled, and in the full light of all the information that could be obtained, in the full light of all that they were told by the ministers, they passed a further resolution declaring that this measure should not be enacted at the present time. I submit that when in this careful, deliberate manner a body of that character, especially a body composed largely of friends of the Government, reiterate and reaffirm their solemn hostility to this measure, there is grave reason why the people of this country should say: You aie proceeding with undue haste.
Other boards of trade are being heard from. We are told at times that the West is thoroughly alive to the desirability of public ownership. Well, the Board of Trade of the city of Regina has passed a resolution strongly objecting to this Bill. The Board of Trade of Sherbrooke, in the province of Quebec, has, as I read in the press, passed a similar resolution. I do not quote any of these as conclusive. I do not for a moment hold up the idea that the board of trade of any community is the wisest judge of all things. But I do feel, as I am sure the country feels, that when earnest business men, not animated by any party feeling, not governed by any desire to injure the Government of the day, men who are known to be friendly to the Government of the day, men who supported the Government of the day in times past and will probably continue to support it-when these men, after full study of the question, )come to the conclusion that this measure is being unduly pressed on the country, I say that is an opinion which the public at large will respect and which, I believe, will have weight through the whole of the Dominion.
I do not want to enlarge upon this question. There is no desire on my part at
least to obstruct this Bill. I have from time to time in discussing the various aspects of it presented my views with all earnestness and all sincerity, and I do not want to repeat myself. I am going to conclude now with a motion which summarizes in brief form much of what I have been saying. I move, seconded by Mr. Murphy:
That BUI No. 33 be not now read a third time, but that the House do come to the following resolution:
That the Grand Trunk Railway system, which the Government propose to acquire, comprises over eight thousand miles of railway line, owned, controlled or leased and operated by the Grand Trunk Railway Company and its subsidiaries;
That the parent Grand Trunk Railway Company has numerous subsidiary companies, and the system includes, besides the railway mileage herein mentioned, the ownership and management of hotels , steamship lines and other property;
That these railways and other property are partly in Canada, partly in the United States and partly in Great Britain;
That the obligations of these companies in various forms run into vast sums, and the financial affairs of the several companies are interwoven by guarantees of securities.;
That the parent Grand Trunk Company and its chief subsidiary the Grand Trunk Pacific Company are admittedly unable to fulfil their obligations to the Dominion;
That the information in possession of the House is insufficient to enable the House and the people to fully understand the complicated affairs of the Grand Trunk Railway system ;
That there has been no inquiry into the affairs of the Grand Trunk system since that which was conducted by the Drayton-Acworth Commission in the spring of 1917, which related to the Canadian railway situation generally, and incidentally discussed the affairs of the Grand Trunk Railw-ay system ;
That the said Drayton-Acworth Commission in their report say concerning the Grand Trunk Railway Company:
" Even if the Government were to relieve them entirely, as suggested by their President, of their unfortunate Grand Trunk Pacifio venture-and, as we have already said, we cannot think that the request can be reasonably justified-it is evident that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not and will not be for some time to come in a position enabling it to pay out any money at all in dividends. We regard the entire share capital as being intrinsically of but small value at the present time. On the basis of present value of maintainable income the fair compensation would be very small."
That of the stock thus described by the Drayton-Acworth report as of small value the Bill proposes to place a perpetual Government guarantee of interest at 4 per cent on about $60,000,000, and to submit the valuation of about $180,000,000 to arbitration.
That the House is of opinion that before taking further action towards the acquisition of the railways referred to the Government should appoint a commission composed of persons of recognized ability and experience in, railway management, railway finance and rail-

way accounting, to make a full inquiry into all the affairs of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and its subsidiary companies, their assets and liabilities, the condition, of the railway lines and their equipment, the physical value of the properties, the sums required to put them in an efficient condition, their estimated earning powers, and generally into all matters in any way relating to the affairs of the companies herein referred to, and to make a full report thereon for the information of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted first to commend the decision of the House that it was unnecessary and uninformative to read the amendment again? The summation of it all is that, at last after three weeks of long drawn out and wearisome debate, chiefly consisting of allegations of haste and of jamming, accompanied by the fact of unnecessary and, indeed, sometimes irritating repetition and delay, the Opposition has come to a policy. The policy of the Opposition divulged only now on the third reading of the Bill is to appoint another Government commission. This, I take it to be the outcome of the new leadership that has recently ascended to place and power in that party. I have sat in this House now for a number of years; but if there is one cry I have heard levelled against the Government more than another in the last two or three years from the hon. gentlemen opposite, it has been that this is a Government of commissions; that instead of doing anything, taking our courage in our hands and going ahead, we appoint always one commission after another to. find things out. It is some comfort to us sitting under those allegations, to find that, however recreant we may have been in that regard, we have at least an Opposition that is ready to go us one better.
Hon. gentlemen opposite say that they have been taunted from this side with being possessed of a desire to go home and quit the business here. The aspersion is quite true; they have been asking to go home for some time. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) now says that the boot is on the other foot; that it is the Government and the members on this side of the House who are anxious to go home. The only anxiety expressed on this side of the House has been to get on with Government business and all other business, to get through and to go home when we get through. The difference between our desire and that of hon. gentlemen opposite is that they want (Mr. Fielding.]
to get home before getting through, and we want to go home only when we get the public business done. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, after, as I repeat, some three weeks of debate,- because this	matter was introduced
on the 10th October and has been pretty much the only subject of discussion ever since, gives us a disquisition on the differences of public opinion in this country on the subject of government ownership, and he says that some very important men in Canada, chiefly in Montreal-from which city, by the way, curiously enough, has generated almost all the opposition to this Bill -are very doubtful about public ownership. We on this side of the House are committing ourselves to it, he says, and he prays us to go carefully and not to go too fast in this matter of government ownership until these douibting wiseacres throughout this Dominion make up their minds on this question, I have a suggestion to make to the hon. member in that regard. He now sits at the feet of the new leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). That new leader of the Opposition comes here, and the first day that he is on his feet in the House he attacks this measure because he says it is not government ownership at all. He tells us that we are not going fast enough into public ownership; that we are delaying for a number of years the right to redeem the bonds which will be issued in payment of the stock which the country will secure. Because this policy does not bring government ownership fast enough, the leader of he Opposition opposes the measure. But his subordinate-the term really sounds inappropriate-from Shelburne and Queen's tells us this afternoon: Oh, please just wait a little while until we have an opportunity to think; this idea of government ownership is so fearfully new to us and so unheard of throughout the country that we want you please not to go too fast in committing the country to this policy.
To the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, who has occupied positions of high trust and responsibility in this Dominion, who has fathered measures of far reaching and, I fear, unfortunate consequences to this Dominion in the periods of his responsibility, whose name, I see, appears affixed to that fateful document that committed Canada to the Grand Trunk Pacific policy in 1903, I put this question:	Has ever a
policy of consequence, great or small, received so lengthy a notification, as ample an opportunity for premeditation and consideration as has this policy now advanced

before the House? Suddenness! Lack of notice! In Canada we have been in government ownership and government operation of railways for years already, as far hack even as Confederation. As years have advanced, we have .passed more and more into those responsibilities, driven by circumstances sometimes faster than many people in Canada would like; but we have advanced along lines of government ownership just as every Government Of subordinate power, just as every municipality of subordinate power, just a-s every public institution in this Dominion has advanced during the last two or three decades in the same direction. As business institutions become public utilities through the march of events and the development and evolution of those institutions, they, gradually it is true, but inevitably come more and more under government operation and government ownership and control. We are only moving along the line over which the ages have moved.
But in any event as to this specific Act, what has been the notice to the Canadian people? On the 15th day of May, 1918, the leader of the Government in this country disclosed to the people of Canada through this House what the Government was directing its efforts towards, and why it was so directing its efforts. In the most ample way he madie /known to hon. members of this House that circumstances were rapidly compelling us to assume ownership, control and operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific. He went farther and stated that circumstances over which he had no control, circumstances, the unfortunate features of which were precipitated upon us by the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite years ago, were driving us, whether we were willing or not, to the goal of government ownership and operation of the Grand Trunk as well. That was on the 15th of May, 1918. Let me read' what he said:
I come now to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I regard it as inevitable, that for many reasons, that road should be taken over by the Federal Government. It is a national enterprise to which the credit of the Canadian people has been committed, and in my judgment it is expedient to sustain it and not permit it to go into liquidation. It is intimately connected with the Grand Trunk Railway system in the East	 The House and the country will be glad to know that the prospects of its traffic seem to be improving and I very sincerely hope that they will improve still more in the early future. That railway cannot be successfully operated without suitable arrangements with the Canadian Northern railway and with the Grand Trunk railway in the East. It cannot pay its .interest charges, and it is utterly impossible for
the Grand Trunk to meet the obligations which' it has undertaken in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific.	,

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The words of Sir Robert Borden, the Prime Minister, spoken on the 15th of May, 1918, or about a year and a half before the introduction of this measure into the House. He went on:
I think, therefore, it is absolutely inevitable that the Grand Trunk Pacific must be acquired.
I can only say that the Grand Trunk would no doubt be willing to hand it over to us to-day if we would relieve the . The Government now proposes fcTlaunen into a new enterprise, that of acquiring me Grand Trunk railway itself.

be, and it is, productive	That the

Hon. ; gentlemen know that we have no system now that can be called a railway system, because we have not the feeders for it such as can make it a success. They want us to stick to something which they know can never succeed, in order that government ownership may be damned forever by failure and their friends and associates may secure a domination of policy which will make well for them but which will not be very good for the people of this country. They suggest a policy of endeavouring to make the Transcontinental pay with no freight to go over it and make the Grand Trunk Pacific pay with no freight to feed it. That is a policy of failure. It is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. A system that is not a system, a commission that would not be a commission; but a repeater, an extravagant and worthless duplication, evasion, drift and delay, dangerous, futile and expensive-all-these things are embraced in the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. Beyond that they have no solution at all; they do not know what to do.
Let me attack the subject from another angle. The late leader of the Opposition took up an understandable position on the 15th of May, 1918. He said in effect on that date: You cannot make a railway system pay unless there are gathering feeders for these great trunk lines. \ railway system that is overloaded with trunk lines and without feeders is not a system at all. It is, in fact, a white elephant, as hon. gentlemen have used the term. But, he said that the Grand Trunk is a great

system; the Grand Jrunk has branches through the United States, traffic is gathered there and distributed through this country, traffic that represents imports of Canada from the United States. It has its great gathering system through Ontario and Quebec and through the north of the Republic, and he plainly saw, as intimated in his statement, that the trunk lines of this country might be supplied with freight and that would bring what would otherwise inevitably be a failure to a condition of success. That is understandable; that is reasonable. What would be his attitude if two years later he found his followers in this House-led on the one hand by a gentleman who says we are not moving fast enough towards Goverhment ownership and led on the other hand by a gentleman who says that we are moving so fast that it staggers him so that he cannot make up his mind and come to a conclusion-saying that we can make a great traffic line'without any system of feeders, that the Grand Trunk is a white elephant, and that we must keep our hands off that railway because the more feeders we secure the less likely we are to make the system succeed. This shows how far hon. gentlemen opposite have departed from the attitude of their leader- and at the dictation of whom? Who is the real leader of hon. gentlemen opposite in this fight? Who represents the real Opposition to this Bill ? Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that they are acting independently. I commented, as I opened my remarks this afternoon on the very curious fact that the opposition to this measure is generated from and revolves around the city of Montreal. It will be remembered that hon. gentlemen opposite, and particularly the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in years gone by referred very sarcastically to the interests of "estimable sirs" and to big business in this country as opposed to the will of the general people. Very strange that in the city of Montreal, the home of the Canadian Pacific, a city that no doubt has benefited largely as a result of being the chief centre and fortress of that railway-very strange I say it is, that there should be found the whole head and front of the offending to the Government policy on this matter. Let the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) not deceive himself. Throughout Western Canada they divide amongst themselves but the people of Western Canada on this subject have made their minds up and there is no mistake where they stand On the question of the Grand Trunk. There is a considerable measure of so called liberalism in Western Canada, there is a farmer movement in that country; they make the same plea as hon. gentlemen to trust the people but they do not stop in actual practice where hon. gentlemen opposite stop. Across the floor of this House they tell us: We have great trust in the people; we have unlimited confidence in their capacity, but we cannot trust them to run a railway; they are not fit to run a great railway system. Although it might otherwise be a splendid thing to unify the Grand Trunk with the Canadian National railways, they say we have not confidence enough in the people of Canada to believe that they can make a success of such an enterprise. Such is not the spirit of Western Canada. Do- not let the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's deceive himself for a moment. He will not find many resolutions outside of Montreal in opposition to this principle. Possibly in the province of Quebec he may get some but I venture to say that he will get mighty few objections if there be first a fair presentation of the case to these people; even in the city of Montreal.
What I bring to the attention of the House is this: Take a look at the railway map of Canada. If there is one argument for this measure that is more forcible, more compelling than another in driving the mind to a conclusion on this subject it is the railway map of this country. Between the great cities of Eastern Canada and between here and the west, everywhere there is duplication, waste of capital and waste of operation and waste of management. Between here and the city of Montreal, between Toronto and North Bay and between points in Western Ontario and Western Canada. What duplication! what cost of multiplication of lines and officers-?

What duplication is there
between Toronto and North Bay?

speechtext: The Canadian National railways go out of Toronto northward towards North Bay, the Grand trunk goes to North Bay. Only this morning I had in my office a traffic expert of the Canadian National railways and he emphasized the condition of affairs between Toronto and North Bay. He told me that there would be an opportunity there for economies, an opportunity for the saving of coal, for the elimination of the small, half loaded train, for the unification of traffic. He explained that it would mean a tremendous saving of money if we could unify these lines and operate them as one system between Toronto and North Bay. You there see trains going out, one on the Grand Trunk, another on the Canadian National destined by shifting later to another line for North Bay and they have to go out only half freighted. Where two trains run between Toronto and North Bay you could run just one and a great saving would be effected. That is only incidental; only by way of example. The same thing exists from end to end of this country, but by unification, by bringing the roads into one system instead of splitting them as they are split up now in their operation is a cause of the embarrassment we find ourselves in to-day, we will have a practicable and perhaps a profitable method of handling the traffic of this Dominion. There is no other solution that has been found; there is no other solution that can be found.

Such are the great advantages to be sought. In addition to that one great object to be attained, there is this:	We
have by this method, and toy this alone, an opportunity to exact from the other partner to the transaction of 1903-4 some share or contribution to the tremendous loss that ensued from that transaction. There is no other method whatever of dividing the loss or .splitting in two the burden of disaster that came out of that unfortunate bargain. By all other means we bear the loss alone. By this means the board of arbitrators will be enabled to assess the value of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and to assess against that the responsibilities of the Grand Trunk for that enterprise, and by taking the difference between its value and the amount of the Grand Trunk responsibilities they will deduct that against the value of the stock of the Grand Trunk itself, and thus the Government will have charged against the Grand Trunk, the other party to the transaction, a share of the loss that pursued that enterprise-a share that the Grand Trunk ought to pay. Now if hon. gentlemen opposite can tell us any other way in which that loss ought to be taken from the Grand Trunk Company can be taken, I would like to hear their plan.
This has not been a matter of sudden adventure, It did take some time and a long time for the Grand Trunk authorities to come to the rather severe terms1-at all events severe in their eyes-that the Government proposed to them. And when the leader of the House rose, on the occasion referred to by the hon. member, and expressed the opinion that hope need not be given up of an early adjournment-even at that hour there was not any final intimation that the Grand Trunk Company were prepared to come to the terms the Government had advanced. speechtext: The crowd is all there.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
It is only a small crowd; they are not all here. Let me remind the Minister of the Interior of the promise he made in connection with the time that he was going to give us. The minister said, page 1026 of Hansard:
Until an agreement was arrived at on each of those details of principle it would have been unfair to intimate that a final adjustment and arrangement was even possible. Consequently it was not competent for the Government to say that it was in a position to announce legislation this session until this very day. Had this legislation not finally been found necessary It was hoped that we might have reached an early termination of the session. Now that it has, the desire of the Government is that the fullest, the lengthiest, if necesasry, consideration be given in this very important matter by Parliament.
There the minister promised that opportunity would be given for the lengthiest possible consideration of this matter. He went on to say that it had been hinted in the newspapers that the Government were going to railroad the Bill through, and that nothing could be further from the intention of the Administration; every opportunity for the fullest possible consideration of the matter would be given. I invite hon. gentlemen to read the minister's speech as it appears on the page from which I have quoted, in which he scouts the idea that there would be any shortening of time for the discussion of this matter or that any advantage would be taken , of hon. members because of lack of time or opportunity to discuss every phase of the Bill. Now, we pleaded that promise to-day and asked for further time; our request was refused, and we are shoved right along.

So far as promises are concerned and expressions of opinion on this subject in the House, I wish to settle a matter of controversy between the leader of the Government and myself and between the leader of the Government and the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) as to what the leader of the Government said about the termination of the session. We might as well know exactly what it is.
I quote from Hansard of October 3, page 858:
Sir George Foster:	There is also this consideration to toe taken into account, that this evening we shall have one opportunity of going through those.
He is referring to certain notices of motion.
Next week we shall have an opportunity to take up those that are for the production of papers and that are germane to the session in this respect: that they give members information which they might be able to use between this and next session and for the next session. This session of Parliament was called, not for private business, but for one special purpose, and it has been confined largely to that, and I think the general sense of the House has been that it should be confined to that. The Peace Treaty has been disposed of, and the legislation necessary in order to carry out Canada's part with reference to that has also been disposed of. Those comprise the important business for which we were brought together; we were not brought together for the purpose of private business. I should hope it is the unanimous wish of the House that the session should end as quickly a possible, and there is no reason why we should not end our work next week. I think both the House itself and the country outside of us will rather be glad if that takes place.
Now, Mr. Speaker, nothing can be clearer . than that the intention on that occasion was that we were to finish the next week. Almost a month has passed and we are not through yet; but the minister will not admit that he gave us to understand that that was to be the case.. There is, therefore, no room for controversy on this point; what the minister said is there in print and anyone e&n see it.
One word about this question of public ownership, 'the minister says that we are going to take this road over as a publicly-owned property in furtherance of the policy of public ownership, and that it is to be linked up with the other railway properties which the Government own. I ask the minister, as did several other members, whether this property of the Grand Trunk, the Grand Tiunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern was to be subject to municipal taxation, and he said:	"No." Now, let
us apply the test of the British North America Act. the plain language of which we cannot dispute. Section 125 says:

No lands or property belonging to Canada oi. any province shall be liable to taxation.
That is what the Constitution says; yet the minister intimates that although this property will be owned by the Canadian people, it will be subject to taxation. Now, one of the advantages of publicly-owned property is that it need not pay taxes. It is one of the reasons why I could understand the Canadian people being favourable to the ownership of a large railway system such as the Grand Trunk-because they-would get the full benefit of its use in connection with the public business of this country; it would not be obliged to pay any taxes. These properties that we own, the Intercolonial and the other railway systems that I mentioned, are either publicly-owned or are not publicly-owned. One of the tests that we would naturally apply to determine this question would be:	Is
the property subject to assessment? If it is subject to assessment, it is privately-owned; if it is not subject to assessment it is publicly-owned. This property, therefore, that we are making such undue haste to bring into public ownership, as hon. gentlemen say, really does not come under public ownership at all; it is to be run as private property.
The minister says that on the 15th of May, 1918, the Prime Minister, in a speech which he made to the House, announced the policy of the Government in connection wdth this matter: that the road was to be taken over. Now, it is not necessary to say that the 10th of September, 1918, is a later date than the 15th of May of the same year; what the Prime Minister said on the 15th of May on a given subject would be considerably qualified by what he said on the 10th of September on the same subject.
We were told by the minister (Mr. Meighen) that a final and definite policy was reached on the 15th May and set forth in the. speech of the Prime Minister on that day. On the 10th September of the same year the Prime Minister sent a cablegram to the Canadian Commissioner in London stating:
Please inform Smithers with respect to his letter 13th August that I have consulted Minister Finance who has just returned as well as my other colleagues. The Government has not power to guarantee proposed note issue without the authority of Parliament and we do not consider it practicable to ask Parliament for such authority. The Government is disposed to assist in every reasonable way the maintenance of company's credit as is evidenced by the advance of one hundred and twenty-two thousand pounds on July 1st and by our offer of 12th July last to advance three hundred and eighty thousand poufids to meet fixed charges upon

terms which were regarded as reasonable but which the company declined. We shall be glad to have any further suggestions from Smithers as to methods of assistance. There is strong objection in Council to any Increase of our offer for the following reasons. It is most unwise and undesirable for a Government without the report of a commission or Board of Arbitration or a vote of Parliament to undertake a large annual payment which would represent the capitalization of eighty or a hundred million dollars. The offer already made is based on the Drayton-Acworth report which affords a sufficient foundation for Government's proposal.
If we go beyond the bounds of that report wo have no certain guide as to what we should propose. Council will not accept either of the offers which iSmithers put forward and unless they receive further offer before end of month they will consider negotiations at an ehd.
We'are taken severely to task because we questioned anything that was said by the Prime Minister on the 15th May in regard to this bargain. On 'the 10th September of the same year he writes to Smithers through the Canadian Commissioner that all negotiations are at an end unless a further offer is made before the end of that month. The blue-book that is given to us contains no such offer, no such proposal, nothing to place between the 10th and the end of September on the lines of those negotiations. Consequently, according to the proposition of the Prime Minister, all negotiations were ended, and yet we are ridiculed by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) because we did not know all about the matter, because we did not continue to think that the offer was all right; that the speech of the 15th May was all right, although the Prime Minister himself brought the whole thing to a conclusion and an end and threw it all to the winds on the 10th September of the same year. That disposes entirely of the accusation and upbraiding of the Minister of the Interior that we knew all about those negotiations, and that we should have complained against them if we had any complaint to make.
The agreement that is before the House to-day is not based upon any part of the Drayton-iAcworth report, and no authority whatever for it will be found in that report. The amendment that is now before us comes right within the attitude of the Prime Minister himself when he says, according to pages 14 and 15 of the blue-book, that it would be unwise for any government to proceed with a transaction of this magnitude involving a capitalization of $80,000,000 or $100,000,000 without a report from a commission. That is the attitude taken by the Prime Minister, the head of this Government, the right hon.
gentleman whom all hon. gentlemen opposite love to follow and quote whenever they find it to their advantage to do so. Nothing could be stronger than the declaration of the Prime Minister when he says: Negotiations are at an end; we made several offers to you; you did not take them; if you do not make a further offer before the end of this September, the thing is all off and there is nothing further about it; before we make any further advance, there should be a full inquiry into the condition of the road. Did that inquiry take place? Nothing of the kind. We have this lamentable condition of things in the House this afternoon. Possibly the best informed minister of the Government on this subject is the Minister of the Interior, and he makes desperate efforts to keep up with the times and the best possible efforts to to fill up the interstices, where he has no information. In those cases he tries to pull things together and to give what might make a presentable case as well as, or perhaps better than any other hon. member on that side. He tells us that we are unreasonable and not sensible in our requests for further information about this transaction, and yet with all his responsibility in connection with this transaction and when he invites us to speak about duplications and lines which should be cut out and how economies could be effected in the running of the road, to the very plain question whether there are two railroads belonging to the Government between Toronto and North Bay, he has to admit that he does not know. That is evidence to me that the Government are not seized of all the information that could well be expected to rest and lodge in them in connection with so important a transaction as this. I have shown very clearly that there is nothing unreasonable in our asking the Government for a further inquiry in connection with this matter; but we are twitted with the remark: Oh, you have been finding fault with the multiplicity of commissions in the past. So we have, and the hon. gentleman who leads the Government added to his many striking phrases when he coined the expression that commissions were as numerous as blackberries and that they were of no service whatever except, that when they reported, their reports were put into dusty pigeonholes and that was the end of them. That is practically what the leader of the Government has said about those commissions. This Government issued possibly hundreds of commissions that were abso-

lutely useless and that had no purpose except that of giving a job to a heeler who was everlastingly bothering them about some job when they had none to give him; they could not give him a position as there was none vacant, and so they said: Oh, well, we will appoint you a commissioner and that will keep you agoing for a while, and when you get through with that, perhaps you will be satisfied or there will be something else. And if he was old, they hoped that he would probably die before he reported in regard to the commission. We had hundreds of commissions under such contingencies; but because there were such commissions and such contingencies, was that a reason why a commission should not be appointed when one was reasonable and proper? This is an occasion when there was every reason to expect that the Government would appoint a commission to look into this matter before they would take over this great railway system which is sixty or sixty-five years old and which has gone through many changes, ramifications and vicissitudes during that time, especially as we have no knowledge of its condition except that we have as to its financial condition the fact that the manager Sir Alfred Smithers came to the Prime Minister of this country asking for help, to endorse his note, so to speak, some time in 1918, to get a little money to keep the wolf from the door for a few years longer. In the last report on the operations and earnings of the road that we have he said that the most heart-rending cries were coming from people all over England who had put their money in this enterprise because he had nothing to give them in the way of dividends; they were everlastingly op-portuning him to give them some return on the capital they had invested in the road. There we have evidence that the road is not in a healthy condition, that it is not paying its way. We have the further evidence that $51,000,000 is required to put the road in proper running condition. We have that statement in the Drayton-Acworth report. When this country was organized and became a Dominion in 1867, the total revenue of the country for the first years of its existence was only $38,000,000. If we were back in those days it would take every dollar of the revenue of Canada to put this road in proper running condition, and we would still be short $13,000,000 of doing it. We are accustomed to talking of millions and billions to-day. We should try to realize what this expenditure would have meant in more normal times, what it would have meant to us, for instance, in 
the first few years of Canada's existence as a Dominion when our revenues were only about $38,000,000. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), a far better authority than I, informs me that our revenues were only $13,000,000 in the very morning of our existence as a Dominion, but to-day the Government think nothing of spending $51,000,000 of cold cash to put the road in proper running condition. We are taking over a road that has not been able to pay any dividends on its stock for the last two years at least, and which has paid dividends irregularly throughout practically its whole life. It is a non-paying proposition. Nobody who had sufficient money to purchase this road today would put his money into the Grand Trunk as a private investment. I would ask my wealthy friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) if he would think it an inviting proposition to put a few of his millions in the Grand Trunk in order to make money. He would say at once: I will appoint a man at your expense, Sir Alfred, to go over the whole road and make a report on every phase of it, to examine every car and every spike on your road before I will put one dollar of my hard-earned cash into this venture.
But when it is the money of the people of Canada it is a different matter. None ol us seem to have a proper comprehension of the thing at all. As long as the money belongs to the whole of Canada, and we should remember we are a very important part of the whole of Canada, we are quite willing to let it go. I repeat there is not a single member of this House, or a properly constituted business man in Canada or anywhere else in the world who would take over this vast undertaking in the haphazard and loose way in which it is proposed we should take it over. We know nothing at all about it. What do we know about the road-bed, the rolling stock, or the equipment generally? Nothing at all, except what is contained in one short letter from some high official of the road who is trying to advance these negotiations as rapidly as possible, who says the road is in good condition. That is all we have. I appeal again to my wealthy friend from Brantford, would he accept evidence of that kind if he was going to buy the Grand Trunk? Certainly not. He would have a thorough investigation made and a business report upon every phase of the property before he would think of taking it over.
It is for these reasons we have moved this resolution. We are asking the members of

this House and the people of this country to consider whether we are not justified in saying that we should go slow in this matter and know what we are buying. We are not obliged to buy this property. There is no foundation for the statement that we are up against it and have to buy this property. Nothing of the kind. If we have properties on our hands that are not paying, whoever would expect to make a fortune by adding to them another property that is not paying its way? To go back to the old illustration of which so much fun was made, if a man has ten cows and cannot make them pay, and gets another two of exactly the same kind and quality, what great chance has he of making twelve pay when he couldn't make the ten pay?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It all depends on the sex of the two.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I made it perfectly clear that they were two cows. Perhaps my hon. friend knows so little about farming he does not know what a cow means.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I was brought up
on the farm and went for the cows when I was a child.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
In view of the present state of the political atmosphere I would advise my hon. friend to learn a little more about farming. I was saying that the roads we now have are not paying. The Intercolonial is not paying, the Grand Trunk Pacific is not paying, the Canadian Northern is not paying. According to figures given me by the Department of Railways and Canals we will have a deficit of at least $49,000,000 or $50,000,000 this year on the Government railways. These are official figures without the slightest monstrosity about them. I was accused the other day of having mathematical notions that were monstrous, but these figures come from the orthodox source I have mentioned. We are going to have a deficit of $50,000,000 on our railways this year, and now when it is proposed to add another railway to the system, we are told we are wasting our breath when ve ask hon. gentlemen who are responsible to the Canadian people for the expenditure of the people's money to inquire into this transaction more fully before we go any further into it.
We are not obliged to buy it, but if it is necessary, in order to make a success of the Grand Trunk Pacific or of the Canadian Northern, that we should own this road, we can immediately get the benefit of it by compelling the company to give us running
rights over the road on proper terms. They owe us something like $200,000,000 and we can give them an opportunity to pay us back some or the whole of that amount by giving us the use of their rails and terminals on rental. We have two lines running across the continent now.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Can the hon. member give the House an illustration of any similarly situated railway system that is operated successfully by the forcing of running rights of one road over another?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I said running rights on reasonable terms; whether they are forced or not is not very material. One railway might not be willing to give another reasonable rights, but the Government are in a position to submit to any company rights within reason and if they do not accept them- then they can be enforced. Perhaps the experiment has not been tried, but I am told that in the United States there is not a single complete system of railway from one coast to the other, and therefore there must be a great many arrangements by which one company secures running rights over the rails of another. We had such an arrangement in this country, for the Canadian Pacific Railway enjoyed running rights over large sections of the Intercolonial for many years. I am not sufficiently acquainted with the details of the matter to-day to know whether they have those rights now or not, but I know that they had them for many years, and the arrangement was an altogether voluntary one on the part of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Who is asking for running rights? We have sufficient roads to carry more traffic than we have. What we want is traffic.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
If we could make money by acquiring the road we could make an arrangement by which we could use the road and give the Grand Trunk an opportunity of paying back their debts by way of rentals. If they are on the verge of receivership now we could say to them : " Don't pay cash. We will give you an opportunity of paying what you owe us by renting to us your terminals and giving us certain running rights which are essential to the success of our road." But, Mr. Speaker, I do not admit that such rights are essential. We have two lines from coast to coast now. We have the Intercolonial running down to the Atlantic, and if we cannot come near enough to making one hand wash the other, so to speak.

under 'these conditions and with the very heavy mileage we now have, I do not for a moment admit that we are going to remove all the difficulties that confront us and make a success of government-operated railways by acquiring the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it the hon. member's plan to help the Grand Trunk to pay its responsibilities to the Grand Trunk Pacific by taking their business from them?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not saying a word about the Grand Trunk Pacific. I presume we are going to take the Grand Trunk Pacific, and, as a matter of fact, we have it now. il simply say that if it is in-dispensible to the success of the Grand Trunk Pacific to connect with lines of the Grand Trunk proper, we could very reasonably expect that arrangements might be made by which its traffic could be carried through to the Intercolonial and thence to the Atlantic coast.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
We can carry it now.
But if the hon. gentleman is going to take the Grand Trunk's traffic how is the Grand Trunk to live?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am contending now that we can carry our traffic, and it is nothing hut camouflage to say that more roads are necessary. We have plenty of rails and terminals and plenty of cars to carry all the freight we have, and it is merely passing the buck to say that we are taking over this railway in order to be able to handle the traffic adequately.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. member does not understand that it is traffic we want. We do not say that we cannot carry the traffic we have. We can carry three times our present traffic, and it is more traffic that we want. The hon. gentleman proposes that we should get it from the Grand Trunk, but how is the Grand Trunk to pay us what it owes1 us, according to the hon. member's suggestion, if it cannot live?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It will not better our condition to take the Grand Trunk and its traffic, for it is not getting enough traffic now to pay. It is not and never was suggested by the Grand Trunk that we were going to get traffic from them. They cannot pay themselves, and in view of that fact how much better off are we going to be by taking their road and its traffic.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We shall be getting the through traffic which we have not got now.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think it can be contended that we have better

facilities for management than this com-; pany of sixty or sixty-five years of age, who surely have learnt the art of running railways if it ever can be learnt. We have no one whom we can put in charge of the rotad who can manage it better than they have done, and with all their traffic in the . United States and elsewhere the whole thing is a huge failure. It is not making money, and any dividends it has been paying have been taken, according to the Drayton-Aeworth report, out of the very life blood of the road. The sum of $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 has been diverted from legitimate expenditure on the road and spread among the shareholders, but the road has not been paying. That is the condition of things which I protest against on behalf of the people and which I submit is sufficient ground for a proper inquiry. We should be in a position to know whether this proposition is a paying one or not, and if it is not a paying proposition, we do not want it, because we do not need it. On the other hand, if it is a paying proposition, a few months' delay until we have secured this desired information will not make much difference. I presume that I am very much in the same position as the Minister of the Interior himself. He admits that he has given us nothing new on the subject. It is difficult, indeed, to get anything new, for we have gone over these points repeatedly. But the proposition is different from our standpoint. We are defending the rights of the people. To the best of our ability we are defending the purses and pockets of the ratepayers of the country, and it is our solemn duty again and again to force upon the attention of the Government, as strongly as we possibly can, our objections to this proposition as it stands. Hon. gentlemen opposite make fun of me because I quote Holy Writ. Well, I am glad that my good friend from Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) comes to my aid occasionally, very fittingly and properly quoting from the same source. Those who profess to be in opposition here are the watchmen on the walls; and the watchman, Sir, is told "Woe unto him if he does not cry out."

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: And they do cry out.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, we, cry out in warning to the people; and particularly, Sir, we cry out in warning to the representatives of those people in this House. We warn the Government againstt this pernicious transaction, and if they do not heed

that warning, then the sword will descend and cut them down, and their blood will be upon their own heads. We need not tell them of their sins and iniquities. Indeed, if we did, they might s'ay, " We may die in our sins but our blood will be on your heads." Hon. gentlemen on this side take good care that if the Government do meet political death, devastation and utter destruction, it will not be because we did not warn them against the errors of their ways and ask them definitely and repeatedly and in an earnest voice to avoid the pitfall into which they are now dragging this country along with them.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I should not like to undertake to make a speech on the merits of this case, as presented by the Government, .after having listened to the eloquent, forceful and convincing address of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). I think he has covered the ground very fully and I shall therefore take but a few minutes in dealing with one or two points which I think have not been touched upon. I was surprised to hear the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), in his outburst before he concluded, refer to the Opposition as defending the rights of the people in this connection. I could not fail to be convinced that he had used the wrong verb.
As a matter of fact, whatever he thinks, or whatever those who are associated with him think, instead of defending the rights of the people both he and they are betraying the rights of the people up to the hilt.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
