speechtext: Except some people.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Except a few people whose names might suggest themselves to us and whom we find it unnecessary to enumerate. He had the amusing assurance to speak of himself as the faithful watchman up on the 'tower switching on the danger signal to warn the public. When he used that metaphor I could not help but think of the words I once heard from the lips of William Jennings Bryan, who was then a candidate for the presidency of the United States. He said: "Woe be to the watchman on the tower if he fails to give the proper signal in the hour of danger when his fellowmen are perishing." A public man to whom his fellows look for leadership and direction is equally guilty if he fails to give honest direction. No greater curse can fall than that which fate reserves for the faithless watchman up on the tower who lures
the shipwrecked mariners to their doom, or the public man who leads the people astray.
This country is in an exceedingly dangerous position at the present time. It is critical almost beyond exaggeration. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us, one after another, that they believe in public ownership. They will argue in favour of public ownership and make out an excellent case, but when it comes to the point they say: " This is not public ownership, and they do their best to find partisan excuses for voting against it. The leader of 'the Opposition points out as one of the reasons why this is not public ownership is that we propose that when the Grand Trunk is taken over taxes shall be paid to 'the municipalities as has been dime by the Grand Trunk in the past. Let me institute a comparison. Take the Government and the city of Ottawa. The Government owns and controls enormous real property interests in the city of Ottawa. It is true it does not pay taxes directly to the city of Otawa, but in lieu of taxes it pays to the city something like $375,000 a year, carries on the important work of beautifying parks, boulevards, etc., and makes other expenditures out of the funds of Canada.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Where does 'the hon. gentleman get the authority for that statement?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I think it was published in the press very recently. It is done by agreement with the city of Ottawa.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Not in lieu of. taxes.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman suggest what, in his view, the large annual payment is in lieu of?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: In lieu of nothing but for the beautification of the city.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Does 'the hon. gentleman really suggest that the Government contributes $375,000 a year to the city of Ottawa for the privilege, if it be a privilege, of keeping the Capi'tol here?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is not for that purpose. This is the capital city of Canada and this commission is appointed for the purpose of beautifying the capital city and we are contributing to it.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: As a matter of fact the hon. gentleman-I do not want to use the word offensively-is squirming.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, I am not squirming.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I am not seeking to be offensive but I used that term because I could not think of any other. There can be no doubt that it is in lieu of the exemption from taxation that the Government contributes this enormous amount of money to the municipality of Ottawa. I cannot conceive of any other reason why it should be contributed. The municipal authorities of Ottawa themselves give that as the reason why this contribution should be made to them. It is not really disputed and we might pass on from that consideration. Suppose that we should adopt the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, this great project of amalgamating the Grand Trunk with our publicly owned system would be thrown into the air. We would never reach a satisfactory conclusion. If you appoint a commission to go into the question you might wait for years before you receive their finding, so great and complex is this problem. This is a very intricate and broad subject. It is absolutely essential in my judgment that there should be as little delay as possible.
Talk of jamming the thing through Parliament, to use the expression of the hon. member for Queen's and Shelburne (Mr. Fielding) it has been before Parliament and the country for over .two years. The Dray-ton-Acworth report, made nearly three years ago by the best experts the Government could secure, recommended this very thing. Surely hon. members sitting opposite must realize that in connection with the railway question the country has been on a great debauch, for twenty-five, thirty or forty years and we have got into this frightful mess. I am not blaming one party more than another; the country itself it to blame for tolerating the blundering, incompetent, or worse, mis-called statesmen or politicians who got us into this mess. Being in that hopeless position, we called in the doctor. If my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has a sick child, he calls in the doctor, and the doctor diagnoses the case, and prescribes the desirable medicine, and if he be a wise father he will follow the doctor's orders. In this railway extremity we called the best doctors we could, there was no politics about it, and the doctors, in the persons of the commissioners who prepared the Drayton-Acworth report, said that the remedy which the Government's proposals embrace, should be applied. Surely three years is a sufficient lapse of time to enable the country and its representatives to consider the question. They have pon-
dered over the question and this decision may be assumed to be the considered judgment of the country. It is true that in the province of Quebec and in the city of Montreal-doubtless in the city of Montreal there is a strong current of public opinion against it. But let me remind hon. gentlemen opposite that the press, financial and otherwise, which seems to be very largely under the influence of the big interests, are pretty generally opposed to this project and the people have had no opportunity of studying or of even learning the facts. I am satisfied that if the Minister of the Interior were to go to Montreal, talk to a thousand of the best and wisest business men of that city, and make the speech that he has made here this afternoon, the men of substance of Montreal would, if not unanimously, at least overwhelmingly, support this Bill. I myself, with my limited ability, would not be afraid of exacting a favourable verdict did I but have the opportunity of pressing the case to the men of Montreal.
What the Government proposes is the only thing to do. We are losing, as the Minister of the Interior pointed out, $25.000,000 a year in the upkeep and operation of these railways that have against our will been dumped into our laps. You could not give the Grand Trunk Pacific away if you tried; the Canadian Pacific railway say they don't want it; nobody wants it, but you cannot afford not to operate it, because if you did not operate it you would have a rebellion in the country that it serves. Large business centres and populations throughout the country have been created by virtue of the construction of this railway. Hon. gentlemen opposite must know that they, or their party, are responsible for this huge, this colossal, this bewildering blunder. This road has been thrown into the lap of the country. It must be operated and so must the Transcontinental. But in connection with that operation we are losing approximately $25,000,000 a year. If we have the Grand Trunk, which was destined to work in connection with these two other railways, I am satisfied that (by practising economies, cutting out superfluous trains, cutting down the number of offices, cutting out officials and making savings in connection with the operation of express and telegraph companies-(because instead of having two telegraph companies as we now have, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Great North Western, we shall have only one and in a hundred other ways enormous economies can be effected, and instead of losing $25,-

000,000 a year, we may be able to break even in a short time. That is what experts tell us. This is the only thing to do. If we want to ruin the country we can go1 on pouring out these tens of millions to the corporations, but by doing so we may strangle for all time the great ideal of public ownership. I thought the leader of the Opposition would not have referred again to the most unhappy and inept illustration he gave to the House the other day about the cow.
He now talks of the country owning ten cows instead of one and he suggests that it would be a mistake to add two more. It makes no difference whether we have ten cows or one cow; at least we have got the cow which was left in our yard, and we are obliged to support that cow. But it is a dry cow, it is producing nothing, not even a pint of milk a year and in addition its upkeep is costing us millions every year. But if we add another animal we can ' probably start the two, or at least start one of them in the direction of producing something, and that is the only way in which we can make a success of public ownership. I see what is in the minds-I shall not say in the mind of the leader of the Opposition nor shall I say in the mind of the former leader of the Opposition-but certainly of some hon. gentlemen opposite. I take it that the two leaders have managed to persuade themselves or are convinced that they are on the right track, but I want to tell all hon. gentlemen in this House who call themselves Liberals, that in supporting such a policy as they are supporting they are endeavouring to destroy for all time, so far as Canada is concerned, the idea of the success of public ownership. We can make a success of public ownership under right conditions; but until Gabriel blows his trumpet we couli not make a success of such public ownership of railways as we have at the present time. The conditions are impossible. And that is what the interests who are behind some people on the Opposition side, a fact perhaps of which they are unconscious, are afraid of. They do not want the Grand Trunk railway to be acquired because with that accomplished public ownership will have a chance for success-it has no chance whatever for success -at the present time. To me, as a man who always believed in Liberal ideas, it is distressing and painful to find my old friends opposing the idea of public ownership and betraying the very cause they profess to have at heart. We can make a success of public ownership because, as I pointed out the other night, it has been
1014 .
made a success in many countries. I omitted to mention then that in all the Australasian colonies the railroads belong to and are operated by the governments. Let me point out to the leader of the Opposition that there, instead of railroads being built to oblige exploiters and railroad buccaneers, they are built where the settlers require them-they are built for the purpose of extending settlement and the development of the country, one of the great and primary ideas of public ownership; the railroads there are a success and the railroad rates are low. I have not got the schedules of rates of those railways with me although I saw them some time ago, but my recollection is that the rates are very moderate, and we can attain that success in Canada at the present time if we have the opportunity. One thing, however, will	have	to be	done. When	thisrailway system is co-ordinated, we will	have	to	lop	off all the	unnecessary mileage and then we will be able to extend moderate rates and give the people of this country Teal service. I can understand why the interests should be opposed to this measure, because when the people of Canada realize that, they have an efficient public-owned railway system and telegraph system of their own it will percolate through the cranium of the average man that he had better patronize his own- system. That is really the explanation of the opposition to this measure. When the Canadian people become proud of their public-owned system they will patronize it, and then we shall have some kind of decent competition in this country. With a great public-owned system of over 20,000 miles of road, reaching every important point in the country, Canada can make a success of her public-owned system. The people themselves will patronize that system and for all time will control rates and dictate the railway policy of this country. Should we allow this system and all the railway mileage of this country to pass into the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, we are bound body and soul to that corporation for the rest of our natural lives. That is why the members on this side, that is why the people of Ontario in great unanimity and the people of the West almost in entire unanimity, are in favour of public ownership. We had railway corporation dictation in the northwestern country for years and years, and the time came when the people practically rebelled against it. I remember myself going out with a revolver in my pocket, as one of a large band
of special police appointed by the city of Winnipeg, to force a crossing where the 'Canadian Pacific company had attempted to bar the entrance of a railroad to relieve The people. We in the West know something about what railway corporation dictation means, and we are determined that that sort of thing shall never happen again. We cannot lose money by consummating this deal-the worst that possibly could happen is that we should save millions every year. And we have not got to pay out any money. Some members and newspapers' who are supporting the Opposition talk about the appalling amount of money we must pay out on this, transaction and they use that argument for the purpose of stirring up opposition and prejudicing public interests with our returned soldiers. We have not got to pay out money at all. It is true that we assume the bond and debenture indebtedness of the Grand drunk railway,	but	the earnings	of	that	system wil pay the interest. Therefore, we are	not	called upon	to	pay	out
this large sum of money, the railway itself will provide the revenue. I repeat, when the railway is amalgamated with the mileage we have at the present time, I have no doubt, and the experts who have studied this question have little doubt that we can make a financial success, of the system instead of going on, as we are doing, losing $25,000,000 a year. If the Opposition could propose any reasonable or acceptable alternative, I for one would be perfectly satisfied as the country has not sought this proposal, but they propose no alternative. They come forward at ihe last moment with the futile suggestion that we refer the whole thing to a commission. Just reflect, Mr. Speaker, where that proposal if accepted would place us: We would be wallowing in the slough of despond and despair before we would receive the report. The time to act is now. Every hour that we continue the operation of the system that we have got-which we had no desire to take over but which was forced upon us-we are losing thousands of dollars. I marvel that hon. gentlemen opposite have not studied this question for themselves. If there was any question about the right thing to do, one could understand their position; but there is no alternative. The proposition has no feasible or even possible alternative. The Government must take the exact course it has set out to take, and by following that course I believe the public-owned system will he made a success.

One word further before I sit down. I find great difficulty in understanding the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. In the old days he was a valiant fighter in the Liberal ranks and he is the man more than any other-although the Old Chieftain must be saddled with his fair share of the responsibility-he is the man that is responsible for driving the Grand Trunk Pacific arrangement through Parliament. The so-called Liberal Government appealed to the country on it and used such arguments as helped to secure a majority in their favour. I myself ran against the western minister in the Laurier Cabinet in opposition to the perpetration of this scheme, because I realized then, although much younger than I am now, that it was a tremendous blunder, and hon. gentlemen opposite know it was a blunder, the whole country now admits that it was a blunder, but it was largely through the specious arguments of my hon. friend, who was then the Minister of Finance, that the country accepted the proposal. Do we find him offering any alternative worth considering to what the Government proposes? No alternative whatever. He is the last man in Canada that should get up and oppose the Government's solution of the existing difficulties in regard, to the railway situation. Ido not-think the country is necessarily clamoring for public ownership of railways with its present- handicap. To help ourselves out of our present unfortunate position we must take over the Grand Trunk system. To find the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) an old stalwart in the so-called Liberal ranks, taking such an attitude makes me wonder sometimes whether he is mentally sound. The idea of the hon. member, an old newpaper man too, t^-in-g the Montreal Star, forsooth, as a mouthpiece of this progressive Union Government. As if an organ of the interests of so pronounced a type could have any influence with any party. Why you could not blast the average Montreal paper asunder from the interests. Think of papers like the Financial Times in Montreal pouring out its wrath and its criticism upon a man whom I regard as the greatest apostle of public ownership in this country, or anywhere else,-the man, living or dead, who in my judgment has done more during the last-quarter of a century for -the interests of Canada than any other man in the Dominion-I refer to Sir Adam Beck! The Financial Times-, last year, heaped abuse and vituperation wholesale upon

this great public servant, this man who has rendered such sublime public service to his country. The Financial Times denounced him because of his work on behalf of the people. That is your Montreal press for you. Why, Lord Atholstan, the proprietor pf the Montreal Star, went West a year or two ago to " study the railway question." How does the leader of the Opposition suppose he studied the railway question-reclining upon a luxuriously upholstered leather sofa in the observation end of Lord Shaughnessy's private car. These are the men who are quoted to us in connection with railway matters. I marvel that thi*' sort of thing continues. I marvel that this House has been kept as it has been kept for the last two or three weeks to debate a proposal which is so clearly and demonstrably sound; a proposal which is so manifestly in the interests of the public. I con* gratulate the Government upon the patience exhibited in explaining and re-explaining, and reiterating its explanations, although the opposition was so futile and puerile and the power behind the throne was so thoroughly suspected and understood. In saying that I do not wish to be offensive to hon. gentlemen'opposite, because many of them believe in the position they have taken.

But mark my words, Mr. Speaker, the time will come and' in Sir Adam Beck's case come swiftly when the pendulum will swing the other \vay and Sir Adam Beck will occupy possibly the highest position in the land. Opposition who loves scriptural allusions. It may be, nay it probably is, that the hand of Providence was behind Sir Adam's reverse and merely brought it about that	he might the more effective'y

Mr. "VIEN: The hon. member has said that by taking over the Grand Trunk we will make money in the operation of the Canadian National railways. Will he reconcile that assertion with the fact, acknowledged by the member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) that for a number of years to come-a number which it is impossible at the (moment to determine-the country will be faced with successive deficits in the management of the Canadian National railways? And how does the hon. member reconcile his opinion as to the profits to be derived from the operation of the Canadian National railways with the experience of United States in connection with their management of their own roads?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I will answer the last question first. So far as the American railroads are concerned, I think it may be accepted that government ownership during the war did not prove successful; they lost money on the railroads. But much of the loss was based on the enormous overcapitalization of these American roads, the doubling .of the co'st of operation and much oif it was due to the fact that the movement of the troops and the carrying on of the war were' the paramount objects which the American Government had in view in taking over these railroads. The giving of service to the people and the earning of dividends was altogether subordinated to the winning of the war, and that is why the state operation of the roads was not financially successful. But let me point out to my hon. friend this: I saw it recently in a white book issued in

England that the British Government realized a surplus of $81,000,000 in the operation of their roads under government ownership during the war.
As to my hon. friend's first question, I will tell him how the operation of these roads can be made successful. He will admit that the greatest folly was perpetrated in the construction of our railroads. Has he ever gone through the Yellowhead Pass? Does he know that there he can stand on the platform of a car on one line of railway and throw a stone a few yards and hit a train running on the track nearby of another line of railway? For hundreds of miles through that district the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific run parallel. Now, one of these lines is entirely unnecessary.

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: How will the taking over of the Grand Trunk remedy that?

subtopic: BILL, PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I will show the hon. member, if he will let me go on; I want to make this explanation. When you take over these roads you have to eliminate hundreds of miles of lines which parallel each other; you have to co-ordinate the system so that we shall not have deficits. If we are going to give public ownership a chance for its life, the Government or Parliament must co-ordinate the systems acquired and retain only what would have been necessary had the lines been built under proper conditions. Put a fair capitalization on what constitutes a real system; wipe all the rest from the ledger. Then, when you have cut the capitalization down to a reasonable and just and proper basis, you will only have to charge freight rates which are sufficient to pay operating expenses and upkeep, and the interest on a reasonable capital. I do not know any other way of making a success of it.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of .representing in this House the constituency of 'Lotbiniere,, the population of which is 90 per cent French Canadian; therefore, I am most happy, in the course of this third session of my parliamentary career, to address the House in my mother tongue, in that beautiful language which resounds on the shores of the St. Lawrence, a language which we keep as the apple of our eyes, and which, to use an expression you have heard within these precincts "partakes of the limpidity of a stream and the resonance of metal."
In rising to discuss the question which is now focussing the attention,, of the House, I do not stand here as a politician or a partisan; I stand here as a representative of the people; and did I wish to put on airs as my hon. friend from Annapolis, I might perhaps say that in addressing the House, I do so as a statesman. As a matter of fact, being once called upon to give [DOT]evidence before a court of justice in Nova Scotia, and being asked, when about to be sworn in, what his functions were, whether

lie was a politician,, he made reply: "No, sir, I am a statesman."
Mr. .Speaker, I harbour in my soul no such pretension, but I may say that in intervening to-day in this debate, I do so in my capacity as a representative of the people, a friend of the people, a citizen of Canada. It is from the viewpoint of the best interests of my country that I shall consider the question which has now been discussed for over three weeks.
I have abstained from participating in this discussion, when the resolution was brought down; I did abstain from any commentary on the principle of the Bill, and during the debate which took place in committee, with all the broadmindedness at my command and free from any political bias, 1 endeavoured to obtain from the Government such information and light as was required, that we might judge the question on its merits and proceed in giving our vote upon a thorough knowledge of the matter.
Mr. Speaker, the country to-day is seething with unrest and discontent. Heaven forbid that I should hold this .Government wholly responsible. Necessarily that unrest is an aftermath of the war; it is, to a large degree, a corollary of that evolution in the field of human thought which is taking place in a world emerging from an epochal conflict. But if that unrest was partly inherent in the conditions which have prevailed these last three or four years,, it has none the less been intensified to a great degree by lack of foresight on the part of the Government in many a field of governmental activity. 'Do not we hear rising from every .quarter, sharp criticisms directed against the Government who failed to bring to bear upon the administration of public affairs that breadth of conception, that freedom from narrowness, that far vision of the statesmen who presided over the destinies of France? From 1911-because the present Administration is after all but a continuation of that of 1911, somewhat modified-the Government has blundered egregiously in railway matters.
In 1903, Parliament had passed an Act sanctioning a contract entered into between the Grand Trunk Company and the Canadian Government. Under this contract the 'Canadian Government undertook to build a National Transcontinental, from Moncton, in New Brunswick, to the City of Winnipeg, in Manitoba. On the other hand, the Grand Trunk Company undertook to build under the name of Grand Trunk Pacific, the other sections of that

system, from Winnipeg to the British Columbia coast. On the completion of that system, it was agreed that the Government would hand over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company that portion of the system known as the Transcontinental by way oi lease, for a period of fifty years, so that the Canadian Government might be relieved of any responsibility, 'during that period, in connection with the management of the Transcontinental.
What happened then? Down to 1911, it was all plain sailing; the Canadian Government built that portion of the system which runs from Moncton to Winnipeg, and the Grand Trunk Company built the sections from Winnipeg to the British Columbia coast. But in 1911, a political revolution occurred in the country, and seizing the reins of power, the present Administration assumed the obligation of going forward with the construction of the Transcontinental. What did they do? Instead of adhering to the terms of the agreement of 1903, they degraded the line, altered the grades, the various inclines of the road; they did not proceed in building the line according to the specifications approved by the Grand Trunk Company; they changed, without the assent of the company, the terminals at Quebec and Winnipeg, and many other important details, in utter disregard of the agreement.
No wonder then that, in 1914, on the completion Of the Transcontinental, when the Government presented it to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and told them: "Gentlemen, this is the railway we have built, this is our National Transcontinental; take it under lease, agreeably to your contract of 1903," no wonder, I say, that the Grand Trunk Company answered:	"You '
cannot force us to carry out the terms of our contract unless you carried them out yourselves; you have altered the specifications, you did not build the road as it should have been built; therefore we consider ourselves relieved of our obligation."'
What did the Government then do? Did they protest? Did they force the Grand Trunk Company to accept the Transcontinental? Did the Government claim that they had carried out their obligations?
No, the Government confessed judgment; they admitted that they had not discharged the obligations binding on them .under their agreement of 1903, and they told the company "You refuse to take over the Transcontinental; we cannot force you to take it over." The Drayton-Acworth report admits that the Government has relieved

the company of any obligation with respect to the Transcontinental.
What happenned then? The Grand Trunk company came forward and told the Government: "Gentlemen, we have built the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the Pacific coast. Never would we have agreed to construct that line had we not had a connecting link between our Western system and the Eastern system. Our Grand Trunk has its terminus at Sarnia, and our Grand Trunk Pacific has its terminus at Winnipeg. Without the linking up of those systems, how could we carry our traffic from Sarnia to Winnipeg?
Under our contract, the National Transcontinental should be the connecting link between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk system. Now, as things stand, we cannot possibly make a success in operating the Grand Trunk Pacific. It will not be a paying enterprise, for this reason that it is an isolated system, without any outlet to the West, and such outlets we should undoubtedly have had, had you carried out the agreement of 1903."
Again, the Government of Canada confessed judgment; they realized that the Grand Trunk Pacific could not be a paying enterprise, deprived as it was of the services of the Transcontinental. What occurred under those circumstances? The Grand Trunk Company, in 1913, applied to the Government for a loan of $15,000,000 to operate its subsidiary company, the Grand Trunk Pacific. They came back before Parliament in 1916, for another loan of $7,081,703; and in 1917	$5,038,053 was
authorized and advanced, and in the spring of 1918 a further loan of $7,471,399 was authorized by Parliament. Every year the Government onoe more confessed judgment that the Grand Trunk Pacific was entitled to Government aid, for the reason that the Government had not respected their agreement of 1903.
Mr. Speaker, in going into those facts, I want to show you that if we are confronted to-day with such an involved situation so far as our railways are concerned, and if we find ourselves face to face with an almost inextricable tangle, the blame falls on those reckless administrators who have shown themselves unable to respect their undertakings entered into with a private company and who, by the very fact, were making it impossible for them to bind the other contracting party to the discharge of its obligations.
To-day. the Government is without a
ghost of a chance to c-ompel the Grand Trunk Company to live up to its obligations. I do not agree with the Minister of the Interior and I am satisfied that were that question referred to a tribunal the Grand Trunk Company would be relieved of its undertakings as regards the Grand Trunk Pacific, the other contracting party having failed to meet its obligations resting on it, under the agreement. Therefore if we are brought face to face with such an appalling situation, the blame is to be laid on the men who now sit in the seats of office.
In 1918, a new situation arose which eventuated in the Government deciding to acquire the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. At this time of speaking, I may say that we are in the dark as to the inner reasons of this transaction. But when the friends of the Government and those who benefit by this transaction shall have swept off the millions which this legislation is going to enable them to pocket, some day we shall know the ins and outs of this business.
The other day, I was told that I was throwing mud and casting reflection on the Government without being able to substantiate my statements; but to day have not we heard the hon. minister of the Interior and the other gentlemen who sit * to your right, Sir, casting on us the imputation that, if we rise at this stage of the debate to register our protest .against the measure which the Government is trying to push through in the dying hours of the session, the reason is that we are tied hands and feet and at the mercy of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the big Montreal interests.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that no body should fling broadcast such a charge and state that we are actuated by pecuniary considerations, without substantiating such a charge, and I challenge the hon. gentleman and those who s'it behind him to prove that we on this side of the House are in the pay of the Canadian Pacific Company or the big Montreal interests.
Actuated solely as I am by a sense of the duty which is incumbent on me and by a desire to discharge it, I say without any fear of contradiction that never have I been approached by the Canadian Pacific Company or by the great Montreal interests; never did I receive a single cent or any other consideration that might sway t'he judgment I have to render in this House.	,
I am quite satisfied that all the hon.

members who sit to your left, Mr. Speaker, are in the same free state of mind .as I am myself, and if the hon. gentlemen on the other side want' to level such charges against us, they are 'in honour bound to substantiate them and to show that their statements are borne out by the facts.
Should they prove to be unfounded, let the hon. gentlemen recant, or public opinion will point the finger of scorn at them and make them swallow their statement as an infaimous lie, a downright slander, without an atom of truth in it.
Now, let us come back foT a few moments to the nature of the charges brought forward by the hon. gentlemen on this side of the House when we stated that out of the deal which the Government is asking the House to sanction friends of the Government and a few financiers in the ring around the Government were going to pocket millions of dollars.
First, we are buying the capital stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. That capital stock is subdivided into five classes: guaranteed stock; first, second and third preference stocks, and the ordinary or common stock.
The .president of the Grand Trunk 'Company, Sir A. W. Smithers and Mr. Kelly have come to a decision. In a letter tabled in this House, they give their assent to the proposed agreement. The Government of [DOT] Canada undertakes to' reimburse at par the $60,000,000 of guaranteed capital, after paying for a certain number of years interest at 4 per cent; further, the Government undertakes to submit to arbitration the value of the four -stocks

the three preference stocks and the common stock.
Undoubtedly, Mr. Speaker, Messrs. Smithers and Kelly and their partners did not subscribe to that agreement without having in hand the majority of the guaranteed and preferential capital stocks for, if they did not have that majority in hand, or under their control, how could they enter into such an undertaking?
Therefore, Mr. -Speaker,, Messrs. Smithers and Kelly and their partners have now in hand a majority of the capital stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Let us try to form an estimate of the value of that capital -stock. In the Drayton-Ackworth report, which has so often been referred to during this debate, there is to be found clearly set out an answer to that question: page lxv:
"We regard the entire share capital of the company as being intrinsically of but small value at the present time. On the

-basis of present value of maintainable income the fair compensation would be very .small."
What was the value of that capital stock? Mr. Speaker, I looked up the market quotations on the London and New York stock exchanges and I find -that previously to this Bill being foreshadowed, the guaranteed stock which ranks first, was quoted below 45 per cent.
On the announcement of the terms of the arbitration agreement, there was a sharp burst in Grand Trunk issues and this guaranteed stock jumped in a few days from 45 to 50, and from 50 to 60 points, and ere long, under cover of the Government guarantee, it will no doubt sell at par, to the great advantage of the present holders. From the market quotations, at this time of speaking, the capital stock of $60,000,000 would not be worth thirty millions, and yet the Government is guaranteeing the entire value of the sixty millions. Moreover, the Government guarantees the entire payment of the stocks of the company, as they will be valued by the arbitration -award. Therefore, it was on good -ground that- I said the other day, that this deal was going to allow some financiers in the ring around the Government to pocket millions. That I stated was grounded on actual facts and on undeniable official documents.
I wish to point out a few inaccuracies in the speech of the hon. Minister of the Interior.
He charged that we availed ourselves of the Drayton-A-ckworth report, when it suited our purpose, and that we laid it aside when it did not serve our end. lOould it not be said that the minister as the pharisee of old sees the mote that is in his brother's eye and sees not the beam that is in his own eye? The minister relies on the Drayton-Acworth report,, when it recommends in the summary of conclusions, clause 41, "that the -entire share capital of the Grand Trunk, -guaranteed and ordinary, be -surrendered to the Trustees in -exchange for an annuity based on a moderate but -substantial proportion of $3,600,000, the -average sum paid as dividend in the last ten years." But the minister brushes aside the report when, after going extensively into facts and figures, the signatories of the report tell us that the sum which ought to have been spent out of revenue for the upkeep and rolling stock of the roa<i was diverted -for dividend purposes.
The minister charges that in quoting the report we wrench certain passages out of

their context. But the hon. gentleman himself easily gets rid of an important part of the report when it does not answer his purpose.
The hon. minister is no doubt right in discarding certain passages of the Drayton-Acworth report, the more so as the authors of this report stultify themselves; but he is wrong in finding fault with us for doing the same thing.
The commissioners appointed to inquire into and report on ^the situation of the Grand Trunk and ""the Canadian Pacific railways have taken cognizance of a mass of documents and established certain facts, but their findings and conclusions do not flow from their premises.
They tell us, in their report, that the Grand Trunk Company did not keep the road into a fair state of maintenance; that the $25,000,000 which ought to have been spent out of revenue for the maintenance of the road and rolling stock was diverted for dividend purposes.
But so much being said, the commissioners recommend that an indemnity be paid, based on the average amount paid as dividends in the preceding years, dividends that have not been earned.
Therefore, I submit that the conclusion and the premises are self-contradictory.
Mr. Aeworth, one of the members of the Royal Commission, was looked upon in Great Britain as a railway expert. He had written "An Essay on the history of state owned railways, in foreign countries."
He came over to Canada, thoroughly imbued with the idea that public ownership of railways was an unmitigated evil. After a rather summary investigation, when it was clearly impossible for him to await the result of exhaustive inquiries, and hailing as he did from overseas, without being conversant with the special conditions which prevail here, he recommends as one of the findings reported that the Government would act wisely in absorbing into theii railway system the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific the Canadian Northern and perhaps other railways. Is this report well grounded?
Some time after the Drayton-Acworth report had been published, Mr. Aeworth was invited to go and give evidence before the Congressional Committee at Washington, which was then sitting.
What did he say, when he appeared before that committee? His evidence would prove interesting reading and it would be no less interesting to see the sudden and new change of front made by Mr. Aeworth, following so close his volte face in the Drayton-Acworth report. Let me quote that extract in English, lest an &x-tempore translation of mine should prove too imperfect: Ottawa despatches contrast the evidence given hy Mr. W. M. Aeworth before the Congressional Committee at Washington with the conclusions embodied in his report on the Canadian railway situation. The two positions certainly cannot be reconciled. Mr. Aeworth in conjunction with Sir Henry Drayton proposed for Canada a stupendous scheme of government ownership of railways. Before the Congressional Committee, only a few days following the publication of his report on the Canadian railway situation he condemned public ownership of railways in unqualified terms. He cited the numerous failures of state owned railways-in Prussia, in France, in Russia, in Italy, in Austria, in India, in Holland, in Switzerland and in Australia. In all these countries Mr. Aeworth declares public ownership of railways has been associated with high rates, inefficiency and stunted development. Summarizing his conclusions he says:
" Railroading is a progressive science. New ideas lead to new inventions; employ new plant, new methods. And this means the spending of much new capital to be recouped by larger economies later on. The state official mistrusts ideas, pours cold water on new inventions, grudges new expenditure." Mr. Aeworth admits that the world's best example of a successfully administered state owned railway is Prussia and at once proceeds to demonstrate that the success is more apparent than real. He says :
" The German government has for many years offered an unyielding opposition to any reduction of rates while it has extracted from passengers and shippers a net revenue which after paying interest in full on the railways debt, yields in normal times a sum of $50,000,0110 towards the general expenses of the government. .	.
" The rosy views of the authors of state purchase (in Prussia) have been far from materializing. They promised reductions of rates and fares and with the great increase in traffic density ought, one cannot but think to have been able to obtain them. The average fare was indeed reduced by 13J per cent between 1900 and 1911. But freight rates were rather worse than stationary. .	.	. The
authors of the purchase further estimated that the profits to be realized would suffice to extinguish the railway debt within 60 years. In fact the sum paid for the acquisition of the railways $205,493,830, and the debt at the date of the last account with one quarter of the period expired so far from being reduced had risen to $270,132,800."
Mr. Speaker, from the evidence given by Mr, Aeworth it follows that in every country where state ownership has been given a trial, has resulted in the piling up of deficits and in deepening more and more the channels through which the people's money is being drained.
Let us still further study that opinion: Mr. Aeworth goes into facts and figures to prove that state ownership in France has been a dismal failure. Summarizing. Mr. Aeworth quotes a French authority as follows:
I(ii2

" From all points of view the experience of State railways in France is unfavourable. The state, above all, an elective administration, cannot be a good commercial manager. It works expensively and is powerless before its employees. The experience which we have recently gained has had at least one result. It has provoked a very lively movement not only against the repurchase of the railways but against all extension of state industry. The result seems to me fortunate. I hope this opinion will be maintained and that not only we but our neighbours may profit from the lesson of these facts."
The Daily Mail does not share Mr. Acworth's sweeping denunciation of the principle of public ownership, nor does it believe that all the state owned railways in the world are as bad as he paints them. The point is that Mr. Acworth has proposed for Canada the very thing he condemns in all other countries where it has been tried. He revealed himself before the Congressional Committee as a violent and indeed prejudiced opponent of government ownership of railways. Yet that is what he would give to Canada and he would demolish one very strong and solvent Canadian railway system in order to accomplish his purpose.
To say that Mr. Acworth is inconsistent is to state the fact mildly. The evidence he gave at Washington completely discredits his report on the Canadian railway situation. And it tends strongly to indicate that Mr. Acworth was not a real influence in the preparation of the report to which he has appended his name.
Well then, Mr. Speaker, when we find so flagrant contradictory statements of facts and conclusions in that report; when we find self-contradictory opinions expressed by Mr. Acworth in his report and before the congressional 'Committee at Washington, are we not justified in subscribing to the statements of fact, but in putting aside conclusions that are not derived from the premises? We are charged by the Minister of the Interior with discarding the report when it suits our purpose to do so. We have scrupulously avoided discarding that part of the report which was grounded on facts, but we have taken the liberty of showing that the conclusions were not borne out by the actual facts.
State ownership of railways is a question that is quite frequently on the 'tapis, and is discussed at great length, whenever a -question having reference to Canadian railways comes up (before the House, whether under the shape of a subsidy for the construction of a new line, or the guaranteeing of a debenture or the payment of an obligation. Invariably, some honourable gentlemen try to make out of this principle of nationalization a little political capital and draw a red herring across the track to cover the misdeeds of the Government, so that the people -may not discriminate between truth and error.

(Continuing in French).
Mr. 'Speaker, before being interrupted by my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) I was stating that a certain group of people in Ontario were advocating in good faith Government-owned railways, .but let me add that they are not a majority.
The majority of those who to-day are in favour of the Grand Trunk being nationalized and taken over by the State are the very people who, while charging us with being in the pay of the Canadian Pacific and the great Montreal interests, sit at the feet of the magnates of the Bank of Commerce and the former owners of the Canadian Northern by whom they are prompted in the expression of their views. These magnates control this Government. They have succeeded in having appointed as managers of the Government-owned railways their most devoted friends, and what they most strenuously want to bring about is the displacing of the financial centre from Montreal to Toronto.
Making of Toronto the metropolis of Canada ,concentrating thither the administration of our railways, such is their dream. They shrink not before the taking over of the Grand Trunk, or even the acquisition of the Canadian Pacific, nothing, regardless of deficits. Were we not right in saying that, in pushing this Bill through, the Government were playing into the hands of their friends?
Far be it from me to suggest that all those who, in the province of Ontario, ad-

vocate the taking over of the Grand Trunk are acting in bad faith. Many advocates of nationalization are intoxicated by the apparent success of the Hydro-Electric. I am personally inclined to believe that it is a wise policy that water powers, as public property should be transformed into electrical energy, to the advantage of the people. As many private companies have abused the privileges granted to them, in indulging in a rate raising orgy to the detriment of the people, it is not to be wondered at that the good people of Ontario should be in favour of the Hydro-Electric commission. But there is a world of difference between developing a water-power and operating a railway.
Once a water-power is transformed into electrical energy, operating expenses are kept very low. There is only the upkeep of the transmission line to attend to, as the municipalities themselves are the distributing agents within their own limits.
But when we have to deal with a railway, it is quite another matter. In the hands of a Government how easily it degenerates into an engine of speculation, favoritism, undue influence and bad administration!
Are railway ties to be bought, the Gov-erment favorite will be neither the most honest merchant, nor the lowest tenderer, but a political friend, regardless of the quality of the railway ties which, owing to poor quality, will soon rot beneath the rails and may cause a train to run off the track, an accident which occurred several times, last year, on the Intercolonial.
When coal is to be bought, they will not consider the lowest tender, but they will look for a friend of the men now seated in power. In manv cases it will supply nothing but coal dust, and the engines fed with this fuel of an inferior quality will be unable to haul the train within the time fixed in the schedules, and often will they be from ten to fifteen hours late, as is well known to those who have had the sad experience of this, while travelling on the government railways.
Every year, the House of Commons will be asked to vote moneys required as a result of the deficits. How will the honourable members of this House be able to get a clear idea of what the management of the railways really is? It would ibe impossible to find out whether it was honest or dishonest, the volume of business transacted being so large.
Secret funds will be created to feed the electoral machine, and in election time pressure will be brought to bear on the
thousands and thousands of employers by the party in power. That the Government operated railways are a source of increasing deficits. I have amply shown, I think, in quoting the evidence given by Mr. Ackworth, the report of the Drayton commission and our own personal experience. But were any further evidence needed, I would find it in the statement made in the Senate by the honourable Sir James Lougheed in answer to a question put by the honourable senator Casgrain.

Well then, I can take it for granted, with the information I have, that the following is the result of the operation of the Canadian National railways by the Government.

under the rules of this House to read statements made by the Government in the Senate, I shall not, at least, infringe any rule in showing that the expectations held out by the Government last year are far from having been realised.
The Government claimed that, with a sound and honest management, with a competent staff, the state owned railway system would be a paying proposition. Now, what return did we get from the operation of the Canadian Northern? For the period extending from the 1st of October, 1917, to the 31st of August, the gross earnings were $93,502,669. The working expenses amount- -ed, for the same period, to $93,188,470. During the same period the Government had to make to the company a further loan of $71,606,463 for construction, betterments and equipment. For the same period, there was a large operating deficit. Up to the 31st of December, the deficit was $4,846,103, and from the 1st of October,
1917,	to the 31st of December, 1917, the deficit reached $2,368,122. From the 1st of January, 1918, to the 31st of December
1918,	the deficit was $14,643,753, and it is

estimated that the -deficit for the present . year will reach $5,587,028.
Decidedly, the rosy views o,f the Government have been far from materializing. But, I ask, Sir, what view are we to take of public ownership, when we consider that these sums do not cover the interest on the cash investment, the reserve fund for wear and tear and renewals, and interest, which no well-advised company would neglect to provide for?
Mr. Speaker, I submit that we have reason to fear that the acquisition of the Grand Trunk by the Government may load this country with additional deficits. Were this railroad a paying proposition by itself, when in the hands of the Government it cannot but increase the already large deficits which the country has incurred as a result of the improvident policy of the Government. Those deficits are making wider and deeper the yawning hollow in the public chest, and that chasm must be filled up. How shall we fill that gap otherwise than by levying a tax on land and the produce of the land, which tax the friends of the Government -are already foreshadowing.
The collection of the enormous taxes which are to be levied will soon set at rest the passing hobby which certain groups of our population have been riding of late. The people will realize, too late, perhaps, who were their true friends; they will understand the falsity of the principles on which the whole policy of the Government is based.
Far be it from me to find fault with the opinions held by the Canadian farmers.
Two years ago, when five thousand farmers came down to Ottawa to meet the Government, they wanted to stand and be heard at the bar of thi-s House so as to give vent to their deep regret on account of the mismanagement of the common weal, and in order to sue for reforms. I apprised you of their wish and it was due to my efforts that we succeeded in having the correspondence laid upon the Table, -after having vainly handed it to His Excellency the Governor General and to yourself, Mr. Speaker. It was only by diint of hard work that we had their memorial praying for a government of the people by the people placed upon Hansard.
To-day should the Government appeal to the farmers, they wouM receive at the hands of those gentlemen, I am sure, the same rebuff which the Tory government in Ontario just got and the Tory government in Ottawa shall soon get. So far as we, [IMr. Vien.]
members of the Opposition, are concerned, we are not afraid of appealing to the Canadian electorate. We have endeavoured to uphold the best interests of the people and we know that they will be grateful to us. We broke none of our pledges and we fully lived up to the faiith placed in us.
We are sometimes reproached with lacking political acumen because we did not discover in time what was the trend of public opinion. Come to the province of Quebec, Sir, and you will see an enlightened, contented and prosperous community, led by its statesmen, its clergymen-its educators for the last three centuries. Those people do not believe that the moon is made of green cheese; they do not act like boy-s who try to blow into the -air empty bubbles which burst and vanish before their eyes. They are wise and practical.
We shall not be afraid to go to them, trusting that they will be capable of discerning truth from falsehood in the matter of the taking over of the Grand Trunk.
When we show them in its true light the agreement submitted to us, the people of Quebec and I dare say the whole people of Canada will deem that we have been deserving of their gratitude and they will still place in us all their confidence.
It wi-ll be -sufficient to explain to them that the proposed transaction gives an inflated value to depreciated stocks and owing to the enhancement of these values, stock-jobbers, manipulators and friends in the ring around the Government are getting the best of the deal, at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers. For the last three weeks, we have been charged with criticizing without suggesting -a better policy. Sir, I have a suggestion to -(make to the Government. We are now encumbered with the Grand Trunk Pacific; we cannot get rid of it; because they did not abide by the clauses of the- agreement of 1903 the Government has relieved the Grand Trunk and deprived themselves of all means of compulsion. Then, there is nothing left for us to do but to resign ourselves to the inevitable and to keep the Grand Trunk Pacific.
The Grand Trunk Company, relieved of its responsibilities towards the Grand Trunk Pacific, can still exist and hold out; let us keep our hands off. In the hands of the Government, it would be another defaulting railway. Some people will retort: " Now, you take over every bankrupt road and you leave out those that -are paying; you accept the whey and leave out the cream."

But, there is no cream in sight. In our hands, the Grand, Trunk will pile up deficits every year. Let us at least avoid those deficits. Does not Mr. Acworth say that in every country state-ownership of railways has been a dismal failure and has involved nations in financial ruin?
Sir, an enormous responsibility rests upon the present Government and the members of this House. Having been elected by the people to uphold their interests, we are the trustees of the national inheritance, and it is our undeniable duty not to betray the mandate we hold through public trust nor to leave it a prey to the financial interests, whether in Montreal or in Toronto. The Government have no right to -allow a few individuals to grow rich at the expense of the people or to jeopardize the legacy transmitted to us by our -ancestors.
What a splendid inheritance and how prosperous it was when, in 1911, the Liberal government handed it to the present Administration ! From 1896 to 1911, Laur-ier had rounded it in a wonderful manner. He had received it in 1896, when the revenue was $35,000,000 and the expenditure forty million dollars. He handed it back in 1911 with a revenue of $225,000,000 and an expenditure of $180,000,000, or a surplus of forty-five millions.
After eight years of management, this Governriient have placed that inheritance on the verge of bankruptcy. Our net debt of $350,000,000 in 1911 now amounts to about two billion dollars and they keep piling it up to an alarming extent.
At a time when all serious-minded people a.re alarmed at the condition of -affairs in this country, our irresponsible -Government -saddles the poor Canadian taxpayer with an additional debt of $500,000,000, without mentioning the $180,000,000 that we shall h-ave to spend on this railway, -so as to put it in good working order and complete the terminal facilities at Montreal and Toronto.
If to -that we add the annual deficits that this foolhardy .adventure is hound to create, we re-alizze at once the precarious situation of our resources.
When travelling through the magnificent, countryside of our beautiful province of Quebec, or of the province of Ontario, I often think of the precious legacy which [DOT]our forefathers have left us.
My thoughts wander back to Champlain leaving behind his beloved France -and- to those heroes who -accompanied him to the hanks of the St. Lawrence, there to establish a new empire in the name of France (and Chistianity.
I think of those fearless missionaries who for one hundred and fifty years, roamed -this beautiful -country -and pushed forward to the very limits of America, bringing the Gospel to the benighted red men,, teaching them the advantages of civilisation.
I -am reminded of our French heroes who during la full century did battle -under extraordinary circumstances, one hand on the plough, while the other carried a gun, cultivating the soil and defending their homes against the savage hordes or the incursions of the English.
I think of those who followed, during the period of British domination and who fought in -a manner less bloody, it is true, but none the less glorious, for the conquest of the political liberty which is o-urs -at the present day.
I think of our Clergy, so intelligent, so zealous; our clergy who guided the education iof this colony from its birth; our clergy to whom we owe what knowledge we have of things both sacred -and profane and the development of -all our institutions; the clergy to whom we owe the preservation not only of the faith of our fathers but -also of the beautiful French tongue which we -cherish so dearly.
When recalling all these things to -my mind, I frequently realize that the imperative duty of the present generation i-s to preserve intact this legacy -conquered at the cost of such toil, such sacrifices -and such devotion; and not only t-o preserve it intact, but to hand it down with-a greater worth and a greater prosperity to- the generations that will succeed us.
What a pity to see -our beloved -country of Canada in the hands of the unfaithful ladministr-ators who govern us ito-d-ay! How -sad to see such a splendid birthright jeopardized by their criminal recklessness!
Let u-s hope that the hour of retribution is at hand; let u.s hope that under the pressure of public opinion this unworthy Government shall at last be forced to render an account of its -stewardship to the people of this -country. What will be the verdict? There is about it no room for doubt. We shall witness a -clean sweep and those who to-day occupy the Treasury benches will be there no- longer. It will be the cleaning of the Augean stables and God knows the cleaning must he thorough, if those who come after them are to find suitable quarters-. We who hail from Quebec do not fear the verdict of -the people and we are loud in our demands that the



day of reckoning wait no longer, so that we may appear once more before our judges for a new mandate. Until then we will continue without fear to discharge our duty watching the Government's actions with the eyes of a very Argus and guarding the public treasury with the tenacity of a Cerberus. And then fortified in the sense of duty well discharged, we .-hall rejoice in the thought that we have done our [DOT] utmost to give to this country once again a clean and honest Administration such as that presided over by the late lamented Bight Hon. Sir W. Laurier.
Without the shadow of a doubt an appeal to the people would mean the defeat of the present Government.
The change can only be for the better, since it is impossible to find a worse Government than the one we have today. The people have all to win and nothing to lose. Under the safe guidance of a progressive Administration this country which we love so much will resume its march, briefly interrupted, towards progress, prosperity and happiness.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak at this stage of the debate I certainly do not intend to cover any extended ground; to my mind it would be impertinent to do so after the very full and comprehensive speeches we have had from both sides of the House. After the clear and incisive statement of the Minister of the Interior this afternoon, and after statements such as were made by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Crerar), it would, as I say, be folly for me to attempt to go generally into this question. I lay emphasis in particular on the remarks of the ex-Minister of Agriculture because occupying, as he does, a seat on the cross benches his speech struck me as a reasoned, sound, and moderate presentation of the facts in this case. However, I want to' refer to one phase which has been mentioned by the members on your left, Mr. Speaker, and which it seems to me has perhaps not been considered with sufficient care-I refer to the acquisition of the $60,000,000 of guaranteed stock, called the "present guaranteed stock." Now it must he 'admitted at once this is no ordinary transaction. It is indeed*, in one sense, a business dealing between relatives and, as one knows, in such matters strict legal rights and rules of business do not prevail. We have, I take it, an absolute legal right, as a creditor of the Grand 
Trunk railway, to proceed to judgment and execution and to drive that road into the hands of a receiver or into liquidation. I think it is generally believed that such a course would be unfair and disastrous. That aspect of the matter was so well dealt with in the remarks of the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that there is nothing I can add to it. But under the circumstances which exist and having regard to the long history of the Grand Trunk railway in this country, the question presents itself: Is the transaction, particularly referring to the present guaranteed stock, a fair and equitable one? Now the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has emphasized that part of the bargain on more than one occasion, and he has stated in the most positive manner that this country is making a gift of from fifteen to thirty millions of dollars to that particular class of stockholders. With all due deference to the hon. member's lengthy experience in finance, I venture to suggest that he is labouring under a fallacy in propounding such an argument, and the fallacy lies in the fact that he confuses market price with intrinsic value. I am quite prepared to admit that in normal times where a corporation is carrying on, and has carried on, a business which pays its way and regularly and steadily earns a rate of dividend, the market price may be taken as an indication of the value of the stock of that company. But let any extraordinary situation prevail, let the times, as they are at present, be out of joint, and the market value is no longer an index. As a matter of truth the market price always presumes a sale, and that market price is an index only of the shares which may from time to time be offered on that market. The law of supply and demand, it appears to me, rules with greater strictness on the stock exchange than perhaps anywhere else in the financial world. Let there he a few shareholders who, by force of circumstance, or for other reasons, must get rid of their stock, and unless there . are at the same time purchasers who are prepared to take on that particular stock the price will inevitably fall and may fall very considerably. So that when we speak of acquiring $60,000,000 worth of stock at the present market price we speak of what is absolutely an impossibility. Most of us will remember that some few years ago a group of the most acute and powerful railway people in the United States desired not to acquire the whole of the stock but to get control of the Northern Pacific rail-

way. Now I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, those men did not start out on that acquisition with a brass band; they were not under the disadvantage which any government is in carrying on public negotiations; they took every precaution that could be taken to conceal their hand in the matter. And what happened ? The Northern Pacific stock which, as I remember, was selling in the 80's in March was selling on the 9th of May at $1,000 a share, and a colossal panic existed in the New York market. So that to obtain by any possible means1- unless using the strictly legal rod which is in our hands-anything like even a con-t"rblling interest in $60,000,000 worth of stock, is an absolute impossibility. It is quite true, as the member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) said, that if he acted as arbitrator or judge and evidence of the market value was brought before him, he would he 'compelled to consider that as one of the plainest evidences of value; but that is only in case of a limited number of shares; when it comes to the absorption or amalgamation of a, concern, wholly different factors prevail. In a small way I have, from time to time, been interested in negotiations towards taking over going concerns, and in no case did either the buyer or seller pay the least attention to the market value, or rather market price, (for market value is a misnomer in a sense), of 'the stock. The things considered were the net assets over liabilities and the earning power of the company. It is only a few weeks since I was called upon to consider taking over a going concern whose stock was quoted on the stock exchange at a considerable figure-a figure very much in advance of this guaranteed stock of which we are speaking-and the terms of that bargain dr proposal were that we should guarantee the public liabilities of the company and should in time, after taking over and winding up, return to the stockholders what equity there might be.
We looked into the matter and came to the conclusion that the proposal was one we could not entertain. But did the vendor for one instant point to the fact that the stock was quoted at the market price? Not at all; he knew, as every business man would know, that in a transaction of this kind covering the total absorption of a company, that was not a factor to be considered.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. 'Speaker, I rise just to make
plain where I stand in respect to government ownership. The debate has been driven into that line, and it would appear that the issue was government ownership or private ownership. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) said this afternoon that the western provinces were solid for government ownership. I think that is largely true, but it does not follow that the western provinces are solid behind the method to be employed in taking over the Grand Trunk. Some mention has been made of protests and memorials from boards of trade against this Bill. In my opinion, if more time was given there would ibe more protests, and it is simply foT the reason that the people of this country do not understand this Bill that we have not had more protests. If reason were needed why more time should be taken to consider this matter I think it was given to the House by theMinisterof Railways himself. In speaking some days ago in this debate he pointed out that in 1903 the Government launched into the Grand Trunk Pacific project, and some time afterward a nigger was discovered in the woodpile; the agreement was not what it appeared to be on the face of it. For that reason I think it would be well to take time, that we may guard against the same mistake this time. This is a tremendous undertaking that will involve this country in very heavy obligations, and I think it would be well for us to take time to consider it. Let the people of this country get to understand the arrangement. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. iRowell) said during the debate that if more time were given, the opposition to this measure would get organized and he seemed to fear that. In my judgment, if public opinion could be mustered in opposition to this measure in sufficient strength to kill it, it should be killed. 1 have confidence in the common sense and good judgment of the people of this country, and do not believe they will be taken in on any propaganda from the Canadian Pacific or any other source.
I am in favour of government ownership, and I am ready to take over the Grand Trunk at the earliest possible moment, but I want to know that we are getting the system at a right price. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) stated the other evening that we should deal, if not leniently with, at least with justice to the British investor. I think every one will agree with that. We do not want to do anything but what is just. He also mentioned that much of this stock is probably held by widows. In this connection let me say, we have widows in this country to look after, and while we want to deal justly with every investor who sees fit to invest his or her money in Canada it does not follow, nor is it good business, that we should go beyond that.
I submit that the contention is unsound -that if we drive a business bargain with the stockholders it will injure Canada's credit or prevent funds from coming in for investment. I believe that the British investor knows exactly the condition of our railway business, he knows the precise financial condition of the Grand Trunk, and he knows very well, also, that if the Canadian people, through their representatives in Parliament, pay more for the concern than it is worth it is not good business; and the truth is that any investor would deliberate for a very long time before investing money in a country that did business of that character. Now, Sir, I think that the Grand Trunk should be taken over, but the price should be fixed on a revenue-producing basis and not on the difference between the assets and liabilities. This may seem a hard bargain to the soft-hearted gentleman who feels so kindly towards the British investor, but it is business nevertheless, and I believe it is the kind of business which the people in the western provinces, who have been rightly termed " public ownership people," desire this Government to make. They want the Grand Trunk taken over, but not at any

price. They want it taken over at the earliest possible moment at the right price.

The ground in connection with this whole matter has been covered so fully that it seems almost futile to say anything further. Some points, however, have been raised in the discussion on the amendment introduced this afternoon which it seems to me it would be worth while to consider briefly before passing from the subject entirely. The amendment suggests that the Bill before the House be not now read a third time, but that the third reading be postponed and a commission appointed to investigate the question of acquiring the Grand Trunk railway and incorporating it with the National system. In other words, it recommends that the whole matter be left in abeyance for an indefinite period. In dealing with the amendment this afternoon the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) stated that there was nothing in the Drayton-Acworth report-a report trans-
mitted to the Government and to Parliament by a committee of experts who made a thorough investigation of the subject- that would justify the Government in the action which it is taking at the present time. In this connection I desire to refresh the memory of the hon. gentleman by a quotation from the Drayton-Acworth report. At page xlvii I find:
We have recommended then that the control of the three companies, Canadian Northern, Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific, pass into other hands ; that the rights of the creditors of all three companies be preserved intact; but that the railways of the three companies be not handed over to, or operated by the Government. It is necessary, therefore, to find some new body or bodies to whom they can be transferred. We think the question, whether there should be one body or more, Is answered by the facts that we have already cited. The Canadian Northern is weak in the East. The Grand Trunk, with the inadequate Prairie branches of the Canadian Northern would be almost powerless to compete in the West with the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific. The natural tendency of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern organizations, if left separate, would be for each to invade the territory of the other. Remaining separate, the Canadian Northern system would need to spend many millions of dollars to obtain an adequate hold on the east in competition with the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk. Remaining separate, the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific system' would need to spend many millions of dollars on new branches in the West, in order to hold its own with the Candian Pacific and the Canadian Northern. And this money would be needed at once, for till it was spent neither organization would possess a complete system. Canada cannot afford all these new railways, and does not need three competitive systems. We recommend therefore that the three undertakings, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk, and the Grand Trunk Pacific he united in one system.
That sentence embodies exactly what the Government is doing or endeavouring to do by the measure now before the House; that is to say, to unite in one whole the 'Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific. The report continues :
To whom then should Its management he entrusted?
After canvassing the possibility of turning the whole group of railways over to a private company in order that private ownership might be given a further test, the Drayton-Acworth Commission puts that idea aside as utterly impracticable and comes to the following conclusion:
Having then arrived at the conclusion that the transfer, of the three undertakings to a commercial company is not feasible, we recommend that they be handed over to a Board of Trustees to control and manage on behalf of, and on account of, the people of Canada. The

trustees should be organized as a company with a nominal capital. But in effect they would be a public authority.
, Is not that exactly what is being done in connection with the co-ordination of the whole of the government-owned railways and the linking up with them of the Grand Trunk Pacific system?

Perhaps the
hon. member may have been so far unable to comprehend the plan that has been suggested as to be led to stand up in this House and say that each of these railways is to be operated as a separate entity in its own corporate existence.
