subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not think that the hon. member can quote anything from the minister which will justify that statement. The minister has stated that the trustees incorporated as a company, just as it has been set out in the Drayton-Acworth report, will take the companies as they are with their complete corporate existence, but he does not say, nor the Government does not say, nor does anybody who supports this measure say, that these concerns are going to be operated independently of one another. They are going to be taken and merged into one complete system. Their corporate existence makes no more difference in regard to them than does the corporate existence of the Central Vermont, or the Great Western, or the Chicago and Grand Trunk as parts of the Grand Trunk Railway system. Nor does it make any more difference in so far as this is concerned than does the corporate existence of the Montreal and Ottawa railway, the Ontario and Quebec railway, the Central railway of Quebec, or the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie as parts of the Canadian Pacific system. They are merged into one complete system for the purpose of operation. If the hon. gentleman does not understand that then it is impossible to get it through his head, and if it is impossible for the argument that has been put forward to sink down into his head, the case from that angle is utterly hopeless.

Marie is merged with the Canadian Pacific, and just as the Intercolonial is merged with the Canadian National railways. The names have not disappeared.

speechtext: OrdeT. I must ask the hon. member (Air. Parent) if he desires to make any remarks, to rise and address the Chair.

speechtext:
The leader of the Opposition says that there is nothing in the Drayton-Acworth report to justify the terms that have been suggested. Again, if he will refer to page 65 of the Drayton-Acworth report, he will see the following statement:
We think this is a case for generosity rather than strict justice. Canada is under obiiga-

tions to the Grand Trunk shareholders, who, in the early days, with but small Government assistance, and in competition with the railways of the United States with their vastly greater resources, built up the first Canadian railway system. In later times the company has had further to meet the competition of heavily subsidized Canadian rivals. And it cannot be said that at any stage of its history the shareholders have obtained excessive profits on their enterprise. On the whole we recommend that, on condition of the surrender by the Grand Trunk Company of their entire share capital, guaranteed, preferred, and ordinary, the trustees grant a certain annuity, charged as a working expense on the whole undertaking of the Dominion Railway Company, for the first seven years, increasing at the termination of that period by something like 40 or 50 per cent. We have left the figures blank as there will be questions of cash in hand, value of stores, etc., which must make the precise figure subject to negotiation, but our meaning is that the first figure should be a moderate but substantial percentage of $3,600,000.
The Government, in the agreement consummated with the Grand Trunk, takes a moderate though substantial portion, of that sum,, $2,500,000. The Government then agrees to ,pay that, or the equivalent of that, to the holders of the guaranteed stock of the Grand Trunk and the -arbitration value, if there is any value, in the first, second and third preference and common stocks of the railway. Is that not carrying out the Drayton-Acworth report?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly not.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I appreciate very fully that the hon. member cannot understand that it is.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not happen to possess all the understanding in the universe. We cannot both have it.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is very reasonable to assume that the hon. gentleman- does not possess it all, but when he is leading a party in this House and taking the position that he is in regard to this question, he should give a little evidence of at least possessing a part of the wisdom of the universe.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext:
There is not a word in it that says it is to be divided.
It says a substantial portion of $3,600,000 shall be given to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk. A substantial portion of

$3,600,000 is being given -to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk under this agreement.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would read section 42, at page 88 of the report, he would see the way in which it was to be divided.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Simply to the shareholders.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: And all the stocks mentioned.

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman say that any stockholder of the Grand Trunk can share in any dividend or annuity before the holders of the guaranteed stock have received their full dividend?

speechtext: I am talking about what is in the report.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Order. These dialogues are very interesting and entertaining but they are not in order.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret if I have transgressed the rules of the House but I simply answered what was said by the leader of the Opposition in discussing the question this afterneon in regard t-o the fact that in his judgment, there was nothing in the Drayton-Acworth report which would justify the action now being taken by the Government or the agreement they have made. I hold that the Drayton-Acworth report justifies them in every single particular, and there has been no argument adduced in this House or from any source to show that the Drayton-Acworth report does not justify the action being taken by tihe, Government. Efforts Shave been made to distort the Dray-ton-Aoworth report and the position the Government has adopted in regard to the method for taking over the Grand Trunk and in regard to what may happen in the arbitration.
Now I come to one final point in reference to what was said by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston), that he is in favour of the government ownership

of railways provided it is carried out on an equitable basis.
From the beginning of this debate, and from the beginning of the discussion in the press, up to the present moment, has any hon. gentleman heard a suggestion as to any possible alternative to taking over the Grand Trunk Railway Company and merging it with the national system under the plan which is now being put forward by the Government?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What about the liquidation of the Grand Trunk railway?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman suggests liquidation. He would force into liquidation all the companies that comprise the Grand Trunk system and put them into the hands of a receiver. Does any hon. member say that it would be possible to put all these forty or fifty companies into the hands of a receiver at one time, and for the Canadian Government to purchase them through the receivership- would it be possible?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: We adopted that method last year in the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Once more I must remind hon. members that the House is not in committee and questions and answers across the floor of the House are not in order.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member was putting a question to the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The hon.
gentleman was absolutely out of order in doing so and no hon. member has the right to answer the question.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is unnecessary to argue the point because hon. members know when they advance the argument that by putting the Grand Trunk system-a system made up of a group of companies-into receivership it would be utterly impossible to acquire that system as one complete unit.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Why so?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
For the simple reason that parts of that system-as the hon. member knows full well-are so desirable to other railway systems, not only in Canada but in .the United States, that the competitive price that would have to be paid for them would be of such a character that the Canadian Government could not acquire them; and the only value of
the Grand Trunk to the Canadian people is in order to meet a condition with regard to the Canadian National railway that was contemplated when the latter was brought into existence. As I have stated a good many times on the floor of this House-perhaps too many times- it is amazing that hon. members who profess to be desirous of seeing the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific made a success can stand up in this House and say they do not want to see these systems linked up with the parent company whose existence was the excuse for their construction. The only reason for the construction of the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific was because the Grand Trunk Railway wanted an outlet into western Canada, and without the Grand Trunk railway-or some other system of equal mileage and serving an equal part of the country-the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific are an utter and hopeless impossibility from a railway standpoint. They cannot be operated without tremendous loss. We are involved in tremendous loss under the operation of them now, and so far no man anywhere has been able to suggest a possible means by which they can be operated unless they are linked up with the feeding systems both East and West.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
If the operation of these
railroads is so hopeless as the hon. gentleman has just remarked, what means can be brought forward by the Government to improve the management and make of these failures a success?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I will give the hon. member the credit of possessing sufficient ability to enable him to understand how they can be made a success.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am open to conviction.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The National Transcontinental and Grand Trunk railways can be made a success providing we can get traffic to haul over them, but we cannot get that traffic unless we have feeders for these lines. You cannot run a trunk line of railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific without feeders. What were the Grand Trunk Pacific and the National Transcontinental projected for; what was the idea behind the scheme? Leaving apart for the moment the question as to whether it is a good scheme or a bad one-a question that has been discussed with sufficient fullness from my standpoint-what was the object in constructing these railways? Was it not

as trunk lines for the Grand Trunk railway into western Canada? What justification was pleaded before the Canadian people for it? Why did the late Charles M. Hays link up the Grand Trunk Pacific proposal with the National Transcontinental if it was not to become a part of the. Grand Trunk Railway system? Hon. members know perfectly well that the whole thing was intended to be part of the completed Grand Trunk Railway system. And yet, now that we have the bare bones and the trunk lines, they wish to have the people of the -country believe we should leave the feeding system that can gather up the desired traffic and turn it over to some other competing railway and leave those lines in their present hopeless and impossible situation. It is needless to labour the question; it is not necessary to study it from the standpoint of a railway man at all; any hon. member knows perfectly well that the Transcontinental cannot be operated by any such method, nor can any other railway. Strip the Canadian Pacific of its branch lines from one end of this country to the other, and what would happen to it? Or turn the traffic gathered on its branch lines to another competing company, and what would happen to it? Could it be operated successfully? What makes the operation of it possible? Surely the gathering system it has from one end of the country to the other; and the Drayton-Acworth report sets out clearly and with absolute definiteness the Grand Trunk as that gathering system in eastern Canada and the Canadian Northern as that gathering system in western Canada, and the two other lines referred to will be linked up with them.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is the hon. member not of the opinion that with the linking up of these railways to which he refers the traffic from the West would be diverted to American ports to the detriment of Canadian ports?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My judgment is just the reverse. My judgment is that by the linking up of these railway systems into one complete system, and by the establishment of a Canadian-owned fleet of -steamships on the Atlantic ocean, the traffic will go through Canadian ports.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What about Portland?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Whether my opinion is justified or not, would the position he any different to-day by the linking up of these systems from what it was when the systems were projected? The Grand

Trunk is running to the same ports now that it was then. What was the object of sending the National Transcontinental to Moncton and to the Atlantic seaboard? Was it not to give the Grand Trunk an outlet to a Canadian port? Well, if that object could not be fulfilled by linking the Grand Trunk up with the National Transcontinental and with the Intercolonial, how is it possible to accomplish it under the original agreement? Because what is being done under this agreement is simply to carry out the original agreement and link the two systems up into one line. And let me say again, whether the original scheme was a good scheme or not, has no bearing on this question -whatever; this is the only possible scheme for making the operation of these railways a success, and without it-

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. member has been interrupted quite often and I do not wish to be unfair to him, but perhaps he will permit me to put one question. In his judgment, is it possible to operate the Grand Trunk with profit and with advantage without using Portland as a terminal?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That has nothing whatever to do with the operation of the Grand Trunk as a part of the Canadian National Railway system. The Grand Trunk is an international system. It gathers a tremendous amount of freight in the United States which is destined for Europe. Very frequently that traffic is hauled through Canada, and that results in the distribution of money throughout Canada. In fact, the freight goes to its destination through the port that the shipper decides it shall be routed through. Because traffic is gathered throughout the western States and routed over the Grand Trunk to Portland, it does not follow that traffic gathered in western Canada cannot be routed over the Grand Trunk and the National Transcontinental to a Canadian port and carried on Canadian vessels to its destination in Europe. The two things are perfectly feasible. The Canadian Pacific has outlets in United States as well as in 'Canada; it is not, for that reason, operating to the detriment of Canada. It is no detriment to Canada that passenger trains from the western States should run over the -Canadian Pacific to Montreal and down to Boston and New York; it is no detriment to Canada that bonded freight should be following 'the same course. And it will not be a detriment to Canada or the Canadian National railways if the same thing be done in the case of our government-

,owned roads. It is perfectly legitimate business, and it makes possible the operation of the Grand Trunk as. part of the Canadian National Railway system for the carrying of Canadian traffic to Canadian ports.
The member for Chateauguay and Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) this afternoon challenged 'the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) with regard to the possibility of eliminating lines where duplications have taken place. Where, he said, are those lines? Let us take one or two examples. One is the line from Toronto to Napanee, where the Grand Trunk and the Canadian National run side by side. The member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) this afternoon referred to the fact that you could throw a stone from the platform of one car to the platform of another car on a different line -in places where the National Transcontinental and Grand Trunk Pacific run through western Canada. Well, there are lines so close together in Ontario that you could almost step from one coach to another of trains running on parallel lines. Between Toronto and North Bay and between Sudbury Junction and Ottawa there is positive duplication.
i Mr. ROBB: (Does my hon. friend claim that two railways run on parallel lines between Toronto and North Bay? Let us have that clearly understood.
Mr. G. iB. NICHOLSON:	Not two, but
three roads, are operated between Toronto and North Bay, the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and the Grand Trunk. They are not running side by side; nevertheless these three systems are being operated between these points, and if the hon. member goes to North Bay and wants to go from there to Toronto he can travel on any one of these three railways. If he travels on the Grand Trunk, he will go down through Huntsville; if on the Canadian Pacific or Canadian National, he goes via Sudbury Junction.
Mr. ROiBB: Eighty miles out of his way.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The more miles he goes out of his way, the greater the number of miles that cars of the Canadian National are unnecessarily hauled, the stronger the reason why we should unite these systems and get rid of unnecessary mileage.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman
*say now that if this proposal is adopted he is going to cut one or two of these three roads? Is that the statement?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If this proposal goes through I do not expect to have anything to do with it. But if it does go through-and I believe it will; I believe that the hon. member in his heart of hearts believes it will go through as the only possible solution of this railway problem-I should say that the management operating such a system of railways as the Canadian National Railway system who would operate competitive trains between one point and another, such as between North Bay and Toronto, should be in a lunatic asylum, and the Canadian people from one end of the country to the other who permit that condition should be with them.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend stated a few moments ago that there were competing lines running direct between Toronto and North Bay. Then he changed his position and said that these lines circled around somewhat, and he admitted that in the case of one of the lines there was a deviation of eighty miles. Now, what I want to know is this: Would he cut off the trains running out by Parry Sound and around by Sudbury? Which of these lines is he going to eliminate and thus deprive the people of these different localities of railroad facilities?	[DOT]

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: It is unnecessary to go into a discussion of details as to how the railway management are going to operate their lines. You do not find the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific operating competitive trains between given points either by a direct or by a devious route. I say that it is unnecessary to discuss even the possibility of the management of the Canadian National Railway system continuing the operation of trains under such conditions. I did not say that in the case mentioned there were direct competing parallel routes. There are three competitive routes between two points; one may be a devious route, but it is there just the same, and the duplication of lines is one of the things that has bedeviled the whole operation of railways in Canada. If we are ever going to make the thing a success, as I believe we can and will, this unnecessary competition must be eliminated.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Which of these lines
would the hon. member eliminate?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That is a matter for the management of the railways. If I were doing it I would run trains between given points by the most direct and economical route; that is the practical wav of

doing it. It is not a question of what road to eliminate; it is a question of eliminating unnecessary services. That is the point.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not familiar with the conditions between North Bay and Toronto, but is it not a fact that the three railways between these two points serve different territories although they begin and end at the same places? In Manitoba the Canadian Northern runs two lines between Portage la Prairie and Dauphin, but the two lines serve different territories.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That is perfectly true so far as local traffic is concerned; what we are discussing now is through competitive traffic-through night trains with sleeping cars, for instance. No one is suggesting that lines be taken up or abandoned where they serve a local community; but it is necessary that these unnecessary trains be eliminated.
I have taken up more time than I had intended, but hon. members have appeared to enjoy asking me questions, and, to be candid, I have had no objection to answering them. But it all comes back to the point:	If hon.
members have discussed the question with any competent railway manager or officer in this country, they know that [DOT]these railways cannot be operated successfully and economically and made to pay unless they are all organized into one system. I care not what scheme you suggest, they must be brought into one system. The leader of the Opposition said that we could accomplish the same purpose by giving the Canadian National railways running rights over the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk running right over the Canadian National railways. Would there be any elimination of unnecessary expense in connection with that? Instead of that, there would be a further multiplication of the cost of operating. The Canadian National railways would have an organization operating its traffic over the Grand Trunk, and the Grand Trunk would have an organization operating its traffic over the Canadian National. The thing is utterly absurd. I asked the leader of the Opposition if he could point to a single instance where a plan of that kind was working successfully, and he was unable to do so, and the reason that he was unable to do so, I believe, was that there is not one in existence.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that there is such an arrangement in connection with the terminals in the city of Montreal and

also one in connection with the terminals in the city of Quebec?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The operation of terminals through a terminal company and the operation of a railway system are two entirely different things. Since the hon. member has brought my attention to. this matter, there has been .in existence for a considerable number of years a plan by which the Intercolonial is running into Montreal and using the terminals of the Grand Trunk. Has any one who has investigated that condition come to the conclusion that it has been a favourable condition for the Intercolonial? Where was the interchange of traffic in connection with that? What happened as regards the Intercolonial? This arrangement was simply putting a millstone around the neck of the Intercolonial as regards its Montreal traffic, and it made it impossible for that railway to compete with other railways successfully.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that there existed an agreement whereby the Intercolonial had all the freight going eastward on Canadian soil brought into the city of Montreal by the Grand Trunk?	-

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Under terms suitable to the Grand Trunk, under an agreement that was put across, if you will allow me to use that term, on the Intercolonial railway-on the Government that was then responsible for the management of the Intercolonial-an agreement that has been beneficial to the Grand Trunk and wholly detrimental to the Intercolonial. That is the condition.

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman's argument is right, does it not show that private management is, therefore, superior to public ownership, because, as he says, the Grand Trunk, a private corporation, has "put across" an agreement on the'Intercolonial which is a public-owned corporation?

subtopic: RILL PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That particular agreement shows conclusively that those responsible for making the agreement on the part of the Grand Trunk railway succeeded in driving with those who were then responsible for the management of the Intercolonial a bargain that was beneficial to the Grand Trunk but detrimental to the Intercolonial. This has nothing to do with the question of public ownership, and the question of public ownership is not being argued at the present moment. I am simply pointing out what is possible of accomplishment in

connection with the operation of these railways. They can be operated only by bringing them together under one system, and the agreement before the House provides for that absolutely along the lines laid down by the Drayton-Acworth report and in a manner that has not been challenged by any hon. member who has spoken on this question. I repeat again that, until some hon. member in this House or some of those outside the House who are attacking this agreement can find some alternative, some way by which the Dominion of Canada can get out from under the obligation with which it has been loaded, not by any one who is endeavouring to put this agreement through, and make it possible for these railways to operate-until they do that, they are simply playing politics and nothing more by attacking this agreement in the manner in which they have done.
